title: OPERATION CIVIL TWILIGHT
situation: {EMPLOYER} hired your unit for a 14-month garrison job on {WORLD}. The base pay is 180,000 C-bills a month — the low garrison rate. Your contract has one clause that could change that: Annex C. If {EMPLOYER}'s civil administrator officially declares a 'state of armed conflict,' your pay triples, you and the employer split salvage 50/50, and the employer starts buying your ammunition and armor at cost. That declaration has not happened, and the administrator will not make it. In 90 days on the ground you have fought 11 armed contacts. They started as small-arms harassment and grew into two real battles against insurgents driving salvaged BattleMechs supplied by {TARGET_FACTION}. That report is 6 days old and solid. But the administrator's office files every one of these fights as 'civil disturbance, category D' — the paperwork label that keeps you on the cheap garrison rate. So you buy your own ammunition at high port prices, patch your own armor out of the unit's money, and pay for a MechWarrior in a hospital bed the contract does not cover. The ground makes it worse. The only 'Mech-rated road between the upper city and the lower port is the Carseval Stair: six switchback terraces, 7.4 km long, climbing at about 9 percent. Anything over 40 tons has to climb it in single file. Your contract requires you to escort 9 more cargo convoys up the Stair, and the insurgents know that schedule. Twice this quarter they have buried remote-detonated charges in the Stair's retaining walls — that report is 4 days old, so assume the current mines have moved. To count as evidence with the MRBC (the mercenary review board that settles pay disputes), your gun-camera footage needs the employer's countersignature within 48 hours. {NPC:employer-contact} signs those reports for the administrator and has started taking 6 to 9 days on purpose — past the deadline. {NPC:intel-source}, a dock cargo broker, sells reliable 12-to-24-hour ambush warnings for 2,000 C-bills each, and the price keeps rising. The math is simple: every month this stays a 'disturbance,' {EMPLOYER} saves 360,000 C-bills, and the insurgents — who have no budget limit — get stronger. Best estimate of enemy strength across the theater is 8 to 12 salvaged light and medium 'Mechs, plus rocket and SRM infantry working out of the lower city; that count is 6 days old, so treat it as a floor. You are being paid to police a war that officially is not a war, and winning the paperwork fight decides whether the unit ends this contract in the black.

objectives.primary: Keep the Carseval Stair open: all 9 scheduled convoys delivered to the upper city with cargo loss under 15 percent.
objectives.secondary: Document every armed contact so it holds up with the MRBC: gun-camera footage plus the employer's countersignature within 48 hours.
objectives.bonus: Capture intact one insurgent-operated BattleMech bearing verifiable {TARGET_FACTION} supply markings, forcing Annex C certification onto the table.

complications.name: Category D
complications.text: The administrator labels every fight a 'civil disturbance,' no matter how heavy the enemy is. At the garrison rate, the employer owes you nothing for ammunition, armor, or medical care. Only the employer can change the label, and keeping it wrong saves the employer money.
complications.mechanicalEffect: After every battle in this contract, you pay for ammunition and armor repair from the unit's own money, at high port prices (ammunition costs 1.4x the book rate). This only stops if a fight is later reclassified under Annex C.

complications.name: The Stair Mines
complications.text: Remote-detonated charges are buried in the retaining walls on terraces 2 through 5. Your sweep teams keep finding last week's mines, not this week's. The insurgents set off the charges when a convoy rolls past, and the walls force everything into single file.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Every convoy-escort battle on the Stair starts with one escort 'Mech or one cargo vehicle knocked out by a wall charge; the escort player picks which lead vehicle it hit. All 'Mech movement on the Stair is single-file, with no room to dodge sideways.

complications.name: Witness Economy
complications.text: Your gun-camera footage only counts with the MRBC if the employer countersigns it within 48 hours. {NPC:employer-contact} has figured out that signing slowly costs you the case. Without the signature, it is just your word against the administrator's files.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The reclassification attempt (DP 'The Classification Fight,' option 1) only succeeds if at least 2 documented fights carry countersignatures, or if you lined up a neutral witness ahead of time (an MRBC field auditor or a ComStar observer).

decisionPoints.name: The Classification Fight
decisionPoints.context: Contact 11 was a full lance-on-lance fight against salvaged 'Mechs carrying {TARGET_FACTION} autocannon ammunition. The administrator filed it as category D before your crews had even cooled the wrecks. At the garrison rate, the unit is now losing about 40,000 C-bills a month against what it actually spends. Annex C could fix that. The only question is what it costs to force the issue.

options.title: File for Annex C reclassification through MRBC arbitration
advantages: If you win, the triple rate applies back to your first documented 'Mech fight — a payout in the hundreds of thousands
You gain salvage rights, turning 11 fights' worth of wreckage into money instead of scrap you need permission to take
The MRBC ruling sets the pattern for every mercenary unit {EMPLOYER} hires after you
disadvantages: The employer turns cold the moment you file: expect slow resupply and the 48-hour countersignature deadline enforced to the minute
The ruling takes 30 to 45 days, and the fighting does not stop while you wait
If you lose for lack of evidence (see Witness Economy), you pay the costs and get a reputation as a price-gouger
options.consequence: The administrator stops pretending to cooperate and starts building a case against you. The ruling lands mid-contract and decides which follow-on mission you get.

costs.risk: Employer relations drop by 2 while the case runs; lose it, and you can forget any contract renewal on this world

options.title: Absorb the costs and bank the goodwill
advantages: Employer relations climb: the administrator knows what you are eating and quietly owes you
No legal risk, no arbitration record, a clean MRBC file
Renewal talks start from 'the outfit that did not gouge us'
disadvantages: You bleed about 40,000 C-bills a month at the garrison rate, and it grows the more you fight
The insurgents read your patience as a fixed budget and push harder to test it
Goodwill is not a contract; the administrator can simply refuse to honor it at renewal
options.consequence: The fighting gets one step harder over the next 60 days. You finish the contract owed a favor that appears nowhere on paper.

costs.resource: ammunition reserve drops 20 percent per extra battle at current prices
costs.risk: The money bleed has no floor; a second hospitalized MechWarrior makes it unrecoverable

options.title: Invoke the cantonment clause — stop escorting convoys until the label is fixed
advantages: Forces the issue in days, not the months arbitration takes, and costs no filing fees
You take zero combat losses while the escort is stopped
It holds up under the contract: clause 9 lets you suspend work when the employer breaks the resupply terms
disadvantages: Convoys get hit without your escort, and the lower city blames you, not the administrator
{EMPLOYER} may call your suspension a breach and freeze your pay account while it argues
An empty escort slot is an open invitation, and the administrator starts taking bids from other units that same week
options.consequence: Within 14 days the administrator either declares Annex C or hires a second unit onto the world, which triggers the SECOND PEN follow-on mission.

costs.resource: 2 convoys go undelivered during the stoppage, counting against your primary objective
costs.risk: Breach countersuit: up to 90,000 C-bills held back until it is resolved

decisionPoints.name: The Intact Prize
decisionPoints.context: Mid-fight on terrace 4, an insurgent 35-ton 'Mech loses gyro control and drops against the retaining wall. It is shut down, the pilot is alive, and {TARGET_FACTION} factory seals are clearly visible on its replacement armor. Capturing it intact is your bonus objective and your best proof for the Annex C case. But the fight is not over, and the convoy is stuck behind you on a mined stair.

options.title: Take it intact — send a lance to recover it under fire
advantages: Physical proof that {TARGET_FACTION} is arming the insurgents — the strongest evidence you will ever get for the Annex C case
The 'Mech itself is worth salvaging even if a court later condemns it
The captured pilot is a second source of evidence who can talk
disadvantages: Recovering it under fire keeps the convoy on the Stair past the 40-minute mark, when the swarm attack hits
A lance tied up in recovery is not guarding the back of the column
If the recovery fails, you took the risk for nothing
options.consequence: Your risk of losing convoy cargo this battle jumps sharply. But if the recovery works, the Classification Fight becomes almost impossible to lose, whichever option you chose there.

costs.resource: 1 lance tied up in recovery for 20+ minutes, leaving the rear of the column unguarded
costs.risk: Convoy cargo losses may pass the 15 percent primary-objective limit in this one battle

options.title: Destroy it and clear the route
advantages: Fast: the convoy keeps moving and beats the 40-minute swarm attack
No recovery risk, no lance tied up
Either way, the insurgents don't get the 'Mech back
disadvantages: The {TARGET_FACTION} factory seals burn with it, leaving you only a photo to argue against the administrator's files
No salvage, no captured pilot
The category D label survives another fight
options.consequence: The convoy gets through clean, but the paperwork fight drags on and the administrator keeps winning it.

costs.risk: The Annex C case loses its best physical proof, so your odds in arbitration drop

options.title: Let the city militia take the capture and the credit
advantages: The administrator gets a public win it has to explain, with {TARGET_FACTION} seals in every news photo
Costs you no risk: the militia handles the slow recovery after the fight
The administrator's deputy now owes you a favor you can call in at renewal or when you need a countersignature
disadvantages: You give up your salvage claim on the 'Mech entirely
The militia may botch the recovery or strip the seals before any neutral party sees them
A favor is not a contract; it is worth only as much as the deputy remembers it
options.consequence: You trade the capture for goodwill: countersignatures arrive on time for the rest of the contract, but you spent a whole 'Mech to buy it.

costs.resource: you give up salvage on 1 light 'Mech (worth about 1,800,000 C-bills as-is)
costs.risk: Once the militia takes it, you lose control of the evidence, and the capture may not hold up as proof for the MRBC

entries.event: A wall charge fires on the convoy on the Stair; the lead vehicle is knocked out. The contact is reported to your command post and the administrator's watch office at the same time.
Your ready lance leaves the lower-city base: 5.1 km to terrace 1 at city speed.
Your ready lance reaches terrace 3. Insurgent fire teams start pulling back downhill through the wall gaps.
The insurgent 'Mech element (2 to 4 machines) either commits or withdraws, based on whether the convoy is still stopped.
Insurgent elements slip away into the lower-city backstreets. The militia checkpoints report nothing, as always.
Swarm point: if a convoy is still stopped on the Stair, backup insurgent cells converge on it.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Any convoy stopped on the Carseval Stair for more than 40 minutes is lost. Clear the route inside 40 minutes, or abandon the cargo and save your escort.

opforSketch.composition: Insurgent cells fielding 8-12 recovered light and medium 'Mechs theater-wide (20-45 tons, mixed condition, 2-4 per engagement), supported by SRM and rocket-launcher infantry in prepared retaining-wall positions. Quality green-to-regular with veteran cell leaders; {TARGET_FACTION} supply improving their availability month over month.
opforSketch.behavior: Ambush from wall cuts on mine initiation; fight for 10-12 minutes maximum; break contact downslope into the lower city. They never defend ground and never engage a formed lance head-on. Their operational target is the convoy schedule and the unit's treasury, not the unit.

forks.name: OPERATION TIER THREE
forks.trigger: Annex C certified — by arbitration verdict, by intact-capture evidence, or by the administrator folding
forks.consequence: The contract re-papers at triple rate with salvage rights. The insurgency, its political cover gone, escalates to open company-strength attacks on the upper city. The unit is now paid for a war and gets one.

forks.name: OPERATION PAPER SIEGE
forks.trigger: Stair closed 72+ hours or convoy quota missed
forks.consequence: Lower-city food and fuel prices triple inside two weeks. The unit is ordered onto riot lines to police the shortage its own paymaster's bookkeeping created, at garrison rate, against crowds that know the unit's name.

forks.name: OPERATION SECOND PEN
forks.trigger: The administrator signs a second mercenary outfit onto {WORLD} (near-certain after escort suspension)
forks.consequence: A rival outfit takes the cantonment-and-depot guard slot at a rate quoted just under yours. Two contracts, overlapping mandates, one renewal. They are competitors, not enemies — that distinction is now load-bearing.

storyElementSeed: A pay clerk staples the month's ammunition invoices behind the engagement report, squares the corners twice, and files the folder under 'civil disturbance' because that is the only box the form has.

resourceGates.appliesTo: File for Annex C reclassification through MRBC arbitration
resourceGates.lackingText: A lawyer takes the case on contingency: you file for 0 C-bills up front, but the lawyer keeps 15 percent of any back-pay you win.

skeleton: garrison force must keep one escalating route open while the employer's sole power to classify each engagement decides whether combat pay, salvage, and resupply clauses ever switch on — every cheap month for the employer is a funded month for the enemy
inspiration: aid-to-civil-power garrison sliding into an undeclared war — Belfast, 1969, the opening year of Operation Banner

title: OPERATION FAIR PRIZE
situation: The cash on this contract is only 120,000 C-bills, set insultingly low on purpose. The real pay is clause 10: it gives your unit the salvage rights to everything in {TARGET_FACTION}'s scrapyard outside {DISTRICT} on {WORLD}. The yard's inventory lists 7 mothballed BattleMechs waiting to be shipped out for rebuild, including 1 assault-class chassis. That list is 19 days old, so treat it as rough — inventories change, but the yard itself will not move. Clause 10 is why you signed. Clause 11 is the trap {EMPLOYER}'s lawyers slipped in: salvage is yours, 'except any item the employer's verification officer marks as war-critical.' That officer is {NPC:employer-contact}, who rides in your command vehicle for the whole job. They can stamp any item war-critical on sight, with no limit on how many. The ground makes it harder. Between the yard and the only landing zone that can take your DropShip lie the Brennac Pans: 11 km of salt flat that floods with 30 to 50 cm of brine on a 13-hour tide cycle. 'Mechs can only walk across the flooded flats at a crawl, and the salt corrodes their leg joints. The wheeled flatbed trucks that must haul out the mothballed 'Mechs — cold 'Mechs cannot walk on their own — cannot cross the flats at all while flooded. The yard has 3 working flatbeds and a lifting crane. Each 'Mech you extract needs one flatbed, 40 minutes to load, and a 70-minute round trip to the landing zone. The tide gives you one dry window of about 7.5 hours from first light. Yard security is 2 light 'Mechs, 4 combustion-engine armor vehicles, and an infantry platoon. The garrison's quick-reaction force — 4 medium 'Mechs, regular quality — sits 31 km away in the {DISTRICT} barracks and will not enter the flooded flats, which helps you as much as it helps them. That report is 11 days old but solid. {NPC:intel-source} confirms the reaction force's standing plan: hold the edge of the flats and shoot anything trying to exit. The employer's cargo DropShip lands at the zone next to yours. Anything the officer marks war-critical loads onto the employer's ship; everything else is yours, but only if it is across the flats before the second tide comes in. In short: 7 'Mechs, 3 flatbeds, one tide, one officer with a stamp, and a clause that lets the employer pay you in the property you just captured.

objectives.primary: Break into the scrapyard and haul at least 4 of the 7 mothballed 'Mechs across the Brennac Pans to the landing zone before the second flood tide.
objectives.secondary: Capture the yard's lifting crane and all 3 flatbed trucks in working order. Without them, no shut-down 'Mech leaves the yard.
objectives.bonus: Get the assault-class 'Mech out specifically, with its factory rebuild markings still on the hull. Proof of its history doubles the resale price.

complications.name: The Stamp
complications.text: Clause 11 lets {NPC:employer-contact} mark any item 'war-critical' on sight. That turns your salvage into the employer's property, and you get only a 10 percent handling fee for it. The officer is rewarded for what they bring home, not for what you keep, so they have every reason to stamp your best prizes.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The officer can condemn any extracted 'Mech they inspect before it loads onto your DropShip (resolve this at DP 'The Officer on the Prize'). A condemned 'Mech pays you only 10 percent of its book value instead of full salvage.

complications.name: Cold Iron
complications.text: The mothballed 'Mechs have dead reactors and sealed-up joints. They are cargo, not fighters, and they only move as fast as the flatbeds and crane can move them. Any fighting near the loading area risks wrecking the very machines that are your pay.
complications.mechanicalEffect: You can move only 1 'Mech per flatbed per 70-minute round trip, and 40 minutes of that is loading under the crane. Any weapons fire within 200 m of the crane or a loaded flatbed risks destroying your ability to keep hauling — the flatbeds have no armor.

complications.name: Brine Clock
complications.text: The second flood tide shuts the flats to flatbeds completely and cuts 'Mech speed in half. The enemy reaction force plans to let the tide trap you, then meet whatever crawls out at the edge.
complications.mechanicalEffect: You have a hard 7.5-hour dry window. Once the flood comes in: flatbeds are stuck wherever they are; 'Mech movement is halved, with a salt-corrosion check every hour in the water; and the reaction force deploys to the edge exits as shown in the reaction timeline.

decisionPoints.name: Reading Clause 11
decisionPoints.context: Before lift-off. The contract is signed, but the operational details are not locked yet. Clause 11 sits in it like a hole in a hull. You can challenge it now, protect yourself against it, or set up the operation so it matters less.

options.title: Renegotiate clause 11 before lift-off
advantages: A cap of one condemnation turns the worst case from a disaster into just a tax
Done openly, it looks like professionalism, not paranoia
It settles the dispute in writing now, instead of in an argument at the crane under fire
disadvantages: A 6-day delay while the change goes up {EMPLOYER}'s chain of command, and the inventory list is already 19 days old
The request tells them exactly which prize you value most
{EMPLOYER} may just refuse and offer the contract to someone else
options.consequence: If they agree, the officer can only condemn one item. But the yard's inventory is now 6 days older, and more 'Mechs may have been shipped out.

costs.resource: 6 more days of aging against an already 19-day-old inventory
costs.risk: 1-in-5 chance the employer refuses and gives the contract to a cheaper outfit that did not read clause 11

options.title: Fly as written, but build a legal case
advantages: No delay: the inventory is aging and the tides are good this week
Recording every capture on gun-camera with timestamps gives you an MRBC case if the officer abuses the stamp
Keeping a lawyer on retainer costs less than one condemned medium 'Mech
disadvantages: Arbitration wins you C-bills after the fact, never the 'Mech itself
The officer acts freely during the mission; your case only helps months later
Win or lose, {EMPLOYER}'s hiring notes now mark you as 'the outfit that sues'
options.consequence: The raid runs on schedule. The real fight over the pay happens later, in arbitration.

costs.risk: The officer can condemn as many 'Mechs as they want during the mission itself

options.title: Sequence the extraction so the best prize reaches the contractor hull first
advantages: Once a 'Mech is in your own bay before the officer inspects it, it is yours in fact, not just in claim
Costs nothing in cash or time
The officer cannot stand on every flatbed at once
disadvantages: Your DropShip lands 3 km farther from the yard than the employer's ship, so every hidden round trip costs 25 extra minutes against the tide
If the officer reports that you did this on purpose, expect an obstruction claim and an MRBC conduct mark
It spends your relationship with the employer to protect the payday
options.consequence: You probably save the assault 'Mech and probably burn the {EMPLOYER} relationship. Future contracts will price your reputation accordingly.

costs.resource: you lose 25 minutes of the tide window per hidden round trip
costs.risk: Employer relations drop by 2 if caught; an obstruction claim holds back the 120,000 cash payment

decisionPoints.name: The Officer on the Prize
decisionPoints.context: The yard is taken. The crane is turning. And {NPC:employer-contact} is standing on the assault 'Mech's foot ramp, stamp already inked, marking it war-critical before it can be loaded. Both clocks are running: the contract deadline and the tide. What you do in the next ten minutes sets the pattern for every prize after this one.

options.title: Comply — load it onto the employer's ship
advantages: Clean hands: you honor clause 11 to the letter and keep the cash payment
Employer relations climb, and {EMPLOYER}'s buyers remember cooperative outfits
No time lost against the tide
disadvantages: The single most valuable prize leaves at 10 percent of its value
You set the pattern: the officer's stamp now hangs over the other 6 machines
Your own crew watched the pay walk away, and that costs you in ways no ledger shows
options.consequence: The officer will likely condemn 1 or 2 more machines. The contract ends profitable on paper and bitter in the mess hall.

costs.resource: you lose 1 assault 'Mech (worth about 9,400,000 C-bills; you get 940,000 as the handling fee)
costs.risk: Crew morale drops, and the precedent invites more condemnations this mission

options.title: Dispute it on the spot — quote the contract's own wording
advantages: The contract defines war-critical as 'operable or quickly made operable'; this 'Mech has no gyro and a dead reactor, so the wording is on your side
You keep the 'Mech moving toward your own ship while the argument happens
It shows you read your own contract, and the officer's stamp slows down for the rest of the mission
disadvantages: The officer files an obstruction claim the moment the ramp lifts
{EMPLOYER} holds back the 120,000 cash payment until the claim is settled
Future {EMPLOYER} contracts come with tighter terms and an oversight officer (a liaison) with more power
options.consequence: You keep the 'Mech while arbitration runs, and you will probably win. But the employer relationship starts a slow decline.

costs.resource: the 120,000 C-bill cash payment is frozen until the claim is settled
costs.risk: Employer relations drop by 2; an MRBC conduct inquiry opens (probably dismissed, but never free)

options.title: Trade — give up the crane and 2 mediums for a signed release on the assault 'Mech
advantages: The officer goes home with bulk tonnage to show off, and you keep the one prize that matters
A signed release holds up in arbitration in a way an argument never does
It turns an enemy into a working partner for the rest of the contract
disadvantages: You give up real value: 2 mediums plus the crane is most of what the trade protects
The officer may take the trade and stamp the assault 'Mech anyway, so get the signature BEFORE the machines load or it means nothing
The crane was a secondary objective, so trading it away hurts your mission score
options.consequence: You reach a split both sides can live with, and the clause 11 pattern at renewal is set by handshake instead of by arbitration.

costs.resource: you give up 2 medium 'Mechs and the lifting crane (worth about 3,800,000 C-bills together)
costs.risk: The trade only holds if the officer signs the release BEFORE the machines load; a spoken deal is worthless and the officer can still stamp the assault 'Mech

entries.event: Yard alarm: the break-in is reported to yard security and the {DISTRICT} garrison at the same time.
Yard security (2 light 'Mechs, 4 armor vehicles, an infantry platoon) forms up at the fence. Their orders are to knock out the flatbeds first, not fight the raiders.
The garrison reaction force (4 medium 'Mechs) leaves the {DISTRICT} barracks, 31 km away by the rim road.
The reaction force reaches the edge of the Brennac Pans. It holds at the exits if the flats are flooded, or crosses if they are dry.
If the flats are dry: the reaction force is mid-crossing, committed, and cannot pull back — the one window where the hunter is exposed too.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The second flood tide arrives at T+7:30 from first light and closes the flats to flatbeds. Any 'Mech not across yet has to walk out at half speed through corroding brine, straight into the reaction force waiting at the edge. Anything still on a flatbed when the water comes stays where it stands.

opforSketch.composition: Yard security: 2 light 'Mechs (20-35 tons), 4 combustion-engine armor vehicles, 1 infantry platoon, regular quality, defensive supplies only. Garrison reaction force: 4 medium 'Mechs (40-55 tons), regular, cohesive, with a commander who has fought on the Pans before. No air support within reach. This report is 11 days old and solid.
opforSketch.behavior: Yard security trades ground for time and shoots flatbeds, not 'Mechs — they know what the raid is for. The QRF will not enter flooded Pans under any circumstance; on dry flats they advance in line abreast with overlapping fields, and at the rim they sit at the exits and let the tide cordon for them.

forks.name: OPERATION BOUGHT BACK
forks.trigger: 4+ chassis extracted under contractor title
forks.consequence: {TARGET_FACTION} wants its machines back before refit makes them someone's lance. Within 60 days, a deniable strike force raids the unit's cantonment to burn what it could not keep — and the unit's new property is the target the unit must now garrison.

forks.name: OPERATION SECOND TIDE
forks.trigger: Tide closes with 3 or fewer chassis extracted
forks.consequence: The brine is eating the pay where it stands. {EMPLOYER} offers a return engagement — cash-only this time, at a rate that prices the unit's desperation — against a yard now garrisoned by the QRF that watched you leave.

storyElementSeed: A tech wipes brine from a mothballed foot actuator, tastes salt on the wind, and re-reads the towing checklist before touching a machine that is not yet anyone's property.

is-kurita.decisionPoints[1].context: The yard is taken. The crane is turning. And {NPC:employer-contact} stands on the assault chassis' foot ramp, stamp inked: 'This machine served the Dragon and returns to the Dragon. The clause is clear. Honor it.' The tide clock runs while honor is defined.

is-davion.decisionPoints[1].context: The yard is taken. The crane is turning. And {NPC:employer-contact} stands on the assault chassis' foot ramp, stamp inked: 'Reads as war-critical to me, Captain. Take it up with procurement — after it's on my Mule.' The tide clock runs while the paperwork argues.

is-liao.decisionPoints[1].context: The yard is taken. The crane is turning. And {NPC:employer-contact} stands on the assault chassis' foot ramp, stamp inked: 'The Chancellor's property was never yours to count, Captain. The clause merely reminds you.' The tide clock runs while loyalty is measured.

resourceGates.appliesTo: Sequence the extraction so the best prize reaches the contractor hull first
resourceGates.lackingText: You have no DropShip of your own at the landing zone, so every prize must pass through the employer's ship, and you cannot avoid the clause 11 inspection. This option is crossed out, with the employer's cargo line shown where your own bay number would be.

skeleton: raiders paid in named salvage rather than cash must haul cold machines across a tide-gated flat while the employer's embarked officer holds authority to condemn each prize at the moment it is won
inspiration: Age of Sail prize law — privateer captures condemned or reclassified by admiralty courts before payout

title: OPERATION STRUCK MATCH
situation: Read Annex B before you sign anything, because Annex B is the whole contract. {EMPLOYER}'s intelligence branch wants to buy the {TARGET_FACTION} garrison's reaction plan on {WORLD} — not a written copy, but the plan itself, performed live and recorded on sensors. They pay per confirmed piece of data. Each tier-1 recording is worth 90,000 C-bills: how fast their small units scramble and what responds first. Each tier-2 recording is worth 240,000: how they deploy a full trinary (about 15 'Mechs), how long their fighters take to get overhead, and when the command network goes live. One tier-3 recording is worth 600,000: the full command net active, a second trinary committed, and their warships handing off sensor data. The employer's analysts need this to time a counter-strike they will not describe to you. Here is the catch: for a garrison to run its reaction plan, it has to have something to react to. That something is your unit. You are the bait. The employer flies you in — one drop, one window. But under clause 7, getting home is 'the contractor's own arrangement.' Nobody planned your ride out, because nobody who wrote the annex expected to be on it. The recording gear is physical: you place 5 sensor pods along the reaction route before you start. To earn the full fee, you have to physically recover each pod; if you only transmit its data by radio burst, you get half fee, because the record is weaker as evidence. The ground is the Anvil Braid: a braided river plain 9 km wide between your drop zone and the garrison's reaction route. You can only cross it at 3 gravel fords, with no cover anywhere and full view from the air. The Braid funnels you in and funnels the enemy reaction onto you — which, the planners note, is exactly where pods 2 through 4 should sit. Garrison strength is 1 'Mech cluster at about two-thirds full, 1 fighter pair ready to launch, and a second pair 40 minutes from launch. That report is 16 days old, so treat it as rough. {NPC:intel-source}, a dockworkers' steward the employer runs, says the garrison commander {NPC:opfor-commander} answers any provocation strictly by the book — and the book is what you are paid to film. One last clause: deniability. The contract demands that nothing left behind can tie this raid to {EMPLOYER}. Your unit markings stay on the ship. The garrison will ask who you are, formally, on an open channel — and how you answer is part of the job.

objectives.primary: Place 5 sensor pods along the reaction route, provoke at least a tier-2 garrison reaction, and deliver confirmed recordings per the Annex B pay schedule.
objectives.secondary: Physically recover all 5 pods for the full fee, instead of settling for the half fee you get from radio-burst transmission.
objectives.bonus: Capture the tier-3 recording worth 600,000 C-bills: the full command net active, a second trinary committed, and their warships handing off sensor data.

complications.name: Paid by the Recording
complications.text: You get paid for confirmed recordings, not for effort, damage taken, or machines lost. A pod overrun before you recover it earns nothing. A reaction the garrison chooses not to perform earns nothing. Your pay comes from the violence aimed at you.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Each of the 5 pods is an objective you can recover. A pod you physically recover pays full fee for everything it recorded. A pod you only transmit by radio burst pays half. A lost pod pays nothing. A reaction tier only pays if you provoke it AND a surviving pod records it.

complications.name: No Ride Home
complications.text: Clause 7 makes your escape your own problem. The DropShip that drops you in does not come back. Whatever lifts you out is your own ship, a ship you hire, or nothing.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Your escape window and pickup point depend on your own transport (see resourceGates). Hiring a pickup into a hostile zone costs 350,000 C-bills and locks the pickup time before the mission starts — the hired pilot will not change it once the shooting begins.

complications.name: The Braid
complications.text: Three fords, no cover, and water everywhere else deep enough to swamp a 'Mech. Crossing while chased means going single file under open sky, and the enemy fighters know the fords better than you do.
complications.mechanicalEffect: All movement across the Braid is limited to the 3 ford lanes, single file, with no woods or cover for 9 km. Enemy fighters get attack bonuses when strafing units in a ford lane. Crossing while a fighter is overhead means taking near-guaranteed losses.

decisionPoints.name: How Loud to Burn
decisionPoints.context: The pods are placed. The garrison knows something crossed the Braid heading east — their scouts are stirring. The next hour decides how big a reaction your pods record. Provoke a small tier-1 reaction and you stay safe but earn little. Provoke a full tier-3 reaction and you pay for the whole contract, but it may cost you a lance.

options.title: Shallow probe — brush the scouts and pull back
advantages: A tier-1 reaction is almost certain: 2 to 4 recordings, 180,000 to 360,000 C-bills, with little risk
You cross back over the Braid before any fighter is overhead
Every machine goes home, and your pickup is unhurried
disadvantages: You earn no tier-2 or tier-3 recordings, so the contract pays less than it cost to run
The employer's analysts only get timing on a response they mostly already knew
{EMPLOYER} marks you as 'cautious,' and that reputation spreads
options.consequence: The mission ends safe and barely breaks even. The employer's counter-strike planners buy their tier-3 data from a different outfit on a different world.

costs.resource: total pay capped near 360,000 against roughly 300,000 in operating costs
costs.risk: A reputation for being 'cautious' costs you contracts on the hiring boards

options.title: Escalate step by step — hold at the route's edge and draw the trinary out
advantages: Tier-2 recordings are the profitable middle of the contract: 720,000 to 960,000 C-bills is realistic
The fight stays at the time and place you chose, with the Braid behind you
You can break off at the first fighter flyover
disadvantages: Holding means trading fire with a trinary that outweighs you
The recall decision comes while pods 2 through 4 are still recording, so leaving early loses your best data
A fighter overhead before you recross is likely, and the odds keep rising
options.consequence: You fight a withdrawal you planned against a force you provoked. Your pay grows the longer your nerve holds against the clock.

costs.resource: ammunition and armor for a long fighting withdrawal, about 120,000 to 200,000 C-bills in supplies
costs.risk: Every 10 minutes past first trinary contact raises the chance of a fighter catching you at the crossing

options.title: Strike the dropport beacon — force a tier-3 reaction
advantages: Hitting the garrison's own infrastructure forces the full response: a second trinary, the full command net, and warship sensor handoff — the 600,000 recording plus everything under it
Tier-3 data is what the employer really wants; deliver it and you name your price on the next contract
The garrison's full commitment, recorded, is also the best map of what will someday hunt you
disadvantages: You have to push deep past the reaction route, with the Braid behind you and fighters certain
It forces the fight the contract does not pay you to survive
Pods only pay if you recover them, and a maximum reaction turns recovery into its own battle
options.consequence: The garrison runs its full reaction plan onto your recorders, and you are standing inside it when the second trinary commits.

costs.resource: expected losses of 1 to 2 'Mechs disabled or destroyed, with no reimbursement — clause 7 covers no equipment at all
costs.risk: The hard deadline shrinks by 20 minutes, because a tier-3 reaction speeds up every timeline event below it

decisionPoints.name: The Batchall
decisionPoints.context: Mid-raid, the garrison commander opens an unencrypted channel, formal as a court summons. This is a batchall — the Clan ritual challenge: name your force, say what you fight for, and bid what you will commit. {NPC:opfor-commander} is offering an honorable, bounded fight: limited forces on both sides, a set prize, no ambush. But your deniability clause says you cannot reveal who you are — and it still binds you, even though it sits in a safe aboard a DropShip that is not coming back.

options.title: Answer honestly and bid — name your unit, fight a bounded duel
advantages: Honoring the batchall buys a limited fight: the garrison commits only what it bid, keeps its fighters out unless bid in, and does not chase you past the agreed terms
This improves your survival odds more than any tactical move you have today
Your name enters Clan records as honorable, which is worth something for decades
disadvantages: It breaks the deniability clause out loud, on the record, so {EMPLOYER} can dock your deniability deposit: 25 percent of your total fees
A limited fight is a SMALLER fight, so the tier-3 recording becomes impossible — the garrison shows you its honor, not its full plan
The employer wanted the reaction plan, not a duel
options.consequence: You likely walk out whole and paid at tier-2 rates, minus the deposit. But {TARGET_FACTION} now knows your name, with everything that means later.

costs.resource: you forfeit the deniability deposit: 25 percent of all Annex B fees
costs.risk: The tier-3 bonus becomes impossible; your total pay is capped at what the limited fight reveals

options.title: Refuse and jam the channel
advantages: No deniability breach: staying silent tells them nothing
An insulted garrison overcommits — refusing the challenge usually pulls the biggest, angriest, most recordable reaction
Best data yield: refusing, plus the beacon strike, is your surest path to the tier-3 recording
disadvantages: The garrison declares you dezgra (dishonored): no limits, no mercy, and open pursuit including free-hunting fighters
That pursuit does not stop at the Braid, or the landing zone, or even the jump point
Every casualty this causes was in nobody's plan
options.consequence: The garrison runs its full plan at full violence for your recorders, and you experience it from the inside.

costs.risk: Open pursuit: your escape losses rise two steps, and the hired pilot's hostile-zone surcharge kicks in (+350,000 C-bills)

options.title: Answer falsely — claim to be a pirate band
advantages: It satisfies the deniability clause to the letter, so your deposit stays whole
A garrison facing pirates sends its second-line units, not its best, so the fight is more survivable
{EMPLOYER}'s fingerprints stay off the world, which is what the bonus quietly rewards
disadvantages: Pirates get the anti-pirate response: tier-2 at best, so the full plan the employer is buying stays mostly hidden
A false batchall, if discovered, is the deepest dishonor the Clans recognize — and salvage left behind is how they discover it
If any machine, pod, or body traceable to you falls into garrison hands, your name is cursed in Clan space for a generation
options.consequence: The lie holds only as long as nothing of yours stays on {WORLD}. The contract pays clean, but the risk rides home in your cargo bay.

costs.resource: your data is capped at tier-2 while the pirate story holds
costs.risk: If discovered (any traceable item left on-world): the COMPROMISED fork triggers and you become hunted prey in Clan space

entries.event: Garrison scouts spot the raid for the first time; the contact report enters the cluster network. Pod 1 records it — tier-1 data.
The ready pair (2 OmniMechs) launches from the garrison line — more tier-1 timing data.
The first star deploys to the reaction route and the fighters start taxiing. Tier-1 is complete; tier-2 begins.
A fighter passes overhead and the Braid fords come under watch — the tier-2 fighter-timing data is captured.
The trinary deploys with the command net active — the core of tier-2, with pods 2 through 4 ideally placed.
If you provoked tier-3: the cluster commits a second trinary and warship sensors hand off. This is the 600,000 C-bill window, open for about 15 minutes.
A second fighter pair launches, free to hunt over the Braid if you did not agree to limited terms.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: At T+75:00 the second fighter pair is overhead with fuel to loiter. After that, nothing slower than a fast 'Mech (8/12 movement) can cross any ford of the Anvil Braid without taking a strafing run. Be west of the water by T+75:00, or the fighters catch you at the crossing.

opforSketch.composition: One {TARGET_FACTION} garrison cluster at roughly two-thirds strength: second-line OmniMechs, with a few front-line machines in the command trinary; 1 fighter pair ready to launch, 1 more at 40-minute readiness; an Elemental point attached to the command trinary. Quality: regular-to-veteran by Inner Sphere standards, even for a garrison. This report is 16 days old and rough.
opforSketch.behavior: By-the-book escalation ladder — point, star, trinary, cluster — each step formally authorized, which is precisely what makes the timing recordable. Will offer batchall on first sustained contact; conduct afterward is governed entirely by the answer received. Against declared pirates: efficient contempt. Against the dishonored: pursuit without boundary.

forks.name: OPERATION TINDERLINE
forks.trigger: Tier-3 recordings delivered and verified
forks.consequence: The directorate's counter-strike gets its timing from your recordings — and the planners want the outfit that has seen the reaction plan performed live riding in the first wave, at a rate that finally prices the risk honestly.

forks.name: OPERATION ASH RIDE
forks.trigger: Personnel or recoverable machines left on {WORLD} when the exfil window closed
forks.consequence: Clause 7 says the ride home was the contractor's own arrangement, and the arrangement broke. Going back for your own — past a garrison that is now expecting you — is nobody's contract but yours.

forks.name: OPERATION NAMED PREY
forks.trigger: The pirate fiction discovered — traceable equipment, pods, or prisoners in garrison hands
forks.consequence: {TARGET_FACTION} enters the unit's name in its grievance rolls. Within the year, a punitive star arrives at the unit's next garrison posting, uninvited by anyone's contract, to correct the record.

storyElementSeed: A sensor tech labels five pods with grease pencil, numbers them like livestock, and does not write the unit's name on anything that might be left behind.

resourceGates.lackingText: You own no DropShip, so you must hire a hostile-zone pickup: 350,000 C-bills, pickup time locked at signing, and no changing the pickup point after lift-off. The brief prints these hire terms next to the clause 7 text, so nobody can claim they read one without the other.

resourceGates.appliesTo: Strike the dropport beacon — force a tier-3 reaction
resourceGates.lackingText: Expendables reserve below the projected burn for a tier-3 provocation: option renders with a deficit warning and the line 'units that cannot afford the ammunition should not pick this fight' in the logistics annex.

skeleton: probe force must be worth reacting to — generating its pay from the violence directed at itself — under a contract that prices each tier of the enemy's revealed reaction plan and prices the force's own survival at nothing
inspiration: Dieppe, 1942 — the reconnaissance in force that bought the defender's reaction plan with the raiding force

title: OPERATION ORPHAN COLUMN
situation: At 0410 local time, {EMPLOYER}'s capital broadcast its surrender to {TARGET_FACTION}, and one minute later your contract stopped existing. Clause 22 (dissolution of your employer) voids everything at once: all duties, all protections, the transport deposit, and the escrow account — which, you now learn, was never actually funded. Your unit is 1,100 km inland on the {WORLD} plateau, mid-operation, with your combat battalion, your repair and recovery vehicles, and 212 dependents and technical staff in one long column you never planned to move under fire. Your ride out is a hired carrier — 3 DropShips under captain {NPC:smuggler-captain} — sitting at the coastal port. The captain has already done the math: the dead government owed a lift fee of 2,100,000 C-bills, the enemy's fighters will close the port in about 9 to 10 days, and the ships are worth more than any sympathy. Pay before lift-off, or accept a lien (the carrier keeps some of your 'Mechs as security), or the ships leave without you. Between the plateau and the coast stands the Cordillera Verais mountains, with only one route your recovery vehicles can survive: the Tessering Gap, 280 km of switchbacks with 3 fortified chokepoints. Those forts are held as of this morning by planetary militia who lowered {EMPLOYER}'s flag before the surrender broadcast even finished. They are now, in effect, toll collectors with heavy weapons. That report is 14 hours old and solid. The enemy's regular forces are closing in: scouts at the plateau edge within 2 days, and a full regiment at the Gap's east mouth in about 6 days (that regimental estimate is 14 hours old and rough). And the enemy is offering terms. An envoy under a truce flag carries a written offer from {NPC:opfor-commander}: hand over all your BattleMechs and armor at the Gap's east mouth, and your people — dependents included — walk to the port under safe passage, keeping only sidearms and pay records. The offer's third paragraph notes that under the surrender terms, any armed force with no recognized employer counts as bandits, and captured bandits are not treated as prisoners of war. Your senior officers are invited to the enemy's field headquarters to finalize the deal. Your column makes 120 km per day with the recovery vehicles, and the port is 9 to 11 days away through the Gap. Your war chest holds 730,000 C-bills. One last thing {NPC:intel-source} flagged before the network went down: the dead government's regional pay convoy — including a gold wagon worth about 1,400,000 C-bills, a share of which is rightfully yours — sits abandoned and unguarded for now at the Vellis way-station, 60 km off your line of march.

objectives.primary: Get the whole column — people, dependents, and combat units — through the Tessering Gap to the port and off-world before the carrier lifts.
objectives.secondary: Arrive with at least 75 percent of your heavy equipment intact. The 'Mechs are the unit's entire wealth and the difference between relocating and disbanding.
objectives.bonus: Grab the abandoned gold wagon at the Vellis way-station (worth about 1,400,000 C-bills) before the nearby militia realize what they are sitting on.

complications.name: No Employer, No Protection
complications.text: With no employer, you lose all the protections the MRBC would normally broker. Anyone captured while armed is treated as a bandit, not a prisoner. From this hour on, no one funds your repairs, resupply, or medical care. Your war chest is all the money you have.
complications.mechanicalEffect: For the rest of the operation, all repair, ammunition, fuel, and medical costs come out of your treasury (war chest: 730,000 C-bills). Anyone captured is removed from the campaign entirely, with no prisoner exchange.

complications.name: The Carrier's Price
complications.text: {NPC:smuggler-captain} is not your enemy, just a businessman. The fee is 2,100,000 C-bills before lift-off. There are other options, and the captain will lay them out politely — he holds every card except time.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Getting off-world means resolving DP 'Who Pays the Lift.' The carrier lifts at the hard deadline no matter who is aboard. If you take the lien: the carrier holds 2 BattleMechs as security, which you can buy back within 12 months at the fee plus 15 percent.

complications.name: Toll Forts
complications.text: Three chokepoints in the Gap, each held by 30 to 60 opportunist militia with heavy weapons, plus a dug-in pair of armored vehicles at fort two. They want to be paid, not to die for it — but if you fight your way through fort one, forts two and three will barricade against you.
complications.mechanicalEffect: At each chokepoint you choose: pay (20,000 to 60,000 C-bills, rising at each fort), fight (a battle one threat step below the seed rating, plus 0.5 days and repair costs), or detour (no battle, but +1.5 days per fort on rough tracks that risk your recovery vehicles).

decisionPoints.name: The Parley
decisionPoints.context: The envoy waits at the plateau edge with a truce flag and written terms. The offer is real, with a real seal, but the third paragraph — the one calling you bandits if you refuse — is the quiet threat under all the courtesy. The invitation for your senior officers to visit enemy headquarters could be simple protocol or a trap. And your column can spare neither those officers nor the two days the envoy says the deal will take to finalize.

options.title: Accept the terms — hand over the 'Mechs, march your people out
advantages: All 212 dependents and every MechWarrior walk to the port under a written safe-passage guarantee, with almost no chance of a fight
The carrier's people-only fee drops to 900,000 C-bills, which the war chest plus the gold can nearly cover
No bandit label, no pursuit, no battles in the Gap
disadvantages: You hand every BattleMech and armor vehicle — about 38,000,000 C-bills to replace, and three decades of building up — to {TARGET_FACTION} at a roadside
Safe passage is only as good as the enemy commander's control over the militia at three toll forts, which is untested
The unit survives as people but dies as a fighting force, and the hiring boards do not list outfits with no 'Mechs
options.consequence: You reach the port intact but with no machines. What walks off {WORLD} is a name, a roster, and whatever the boards will pay for either.

costs.resource: you give up all heavy equipment (about 38,000,000 C-bills to replace)
costs.risk: The officers attending the meeting walk into the enemy's camp under guarantees no one can enforce

options.title: Stall the talks while the column keeps moving
advantages: Every day you spend 'negotiating' is a day the enemy regiment waits at the plateau edge for your answer
2 to 3 days gained can get the column past fort one before the pursuit hardens
You commit to nothing; the offer stays open right up until they revoke it
disadvantages: The envoy has eyes, and a column that keeps moving while it negotiates raises too much dust to hide
When the enemy sees through it, they revoke safe passage angrily, and the bandit label now comes with a real grievance behind it
Your officers are running these talks from a moving headquarters, and doing it badly
options.consequence: You buy 2 to 3 days at the cost of the enemy's good faith. From the moment they catch on, the pursuit runs one step hotter than it would have.

costs.resource: the envoy's goodwill, gone for good once they catch on
costs.risk: Pursuit threat rises 1 step after they see through it, and no future talks will be offered

options.title: Refuse outright and race for the Gap
advantages: No risk of losing your leadership, no officers in anyone's camp, no pretense to manage
The column moves at full speed from hour one — the only option that clearly beats the enemy regiment to the east mouth
On the boards, 'they refused and brought their 'Mechs home' is the sentence that builds a unit's next decade
disadvantages: All three toll forts now know a declared bandit column is coming and set their prices to match
Every fight from here on has no prisoner protections and no repair money beyond the war chest
The enemy reads your refusal as contempt, and {NPC:opfor-commander} takes personal charge of the pursuit
options.consequence: Now it is a straight race: 120 km per day against a closing regiment, three forts, and a carrier deadline that does not care who wins.

costs.resource: the war chest covers all Gap costs, whether tolls or repairs
costs.risk: You risk a fight at every chokepoint, and the bandit label is active for the whole march

decisionPoints.name: Who Pays the Lift
decisionPoints.context: The column is at the port, or close enough to bargain as if it is. {NPC:smuggler-captain} receives your command staff aboard with coffee and a printed fee schedule. The number has not changed: 2,100,000. But the timeline has — the enemy fighters will close the port in single-digit hours now. The captain is friendly, but he will not lower the price a single C-bill.

options.title: Pay in full from the treasury
advantages: You own your own future free and clear: no liens, no held 'Mechs, no debt riding home in the cargo bay
The captain remembers units that pay, and word travels among carriers for years
Negotiations end and loading starts within the hour
disadvantages: It takes 2,100,000, which the war chest cannot cover without the gold bonus — and maybe not even with it
You lift solvent and land broke: no repair money, no deposit for the next contract, no margin
Every C-bill spent here was your rebuild fund
options.consequence: You arrive at your next port whole, debt-free, and nearly broke — a hard quarter, but your own.

costs.risk: Your treasury drops below its operating minimum; you sign the next contract hungry, and hungry outfits sign bad deals

options.title: Accept the lien — let the carrier hold 2 'Mechs as security
advantages: Lifts the whole column today for 600,000 down
The held 'Mechs are not sold; you can buy them back within 12 months at the fee plus 15 percent
Keeps your treasury for the rebuild and the next contract deposit
disadvantages: The carrier picks which 2 'Mechs to hold, and carriers pick well
Buying them back costs 2,415,000 total — a bet that next year goes better than this one
A lien on a mercenary unit's 'Mechs is public record, and the boards read it as a sign of trouble
options.consequence: Two 'Mechs ride in a sealed, locked bay. You have a year to earn them back, or watch them sold at auction with your crest still on them.

costs.resource: 2 BattleMechs held by the carrier for up to 12 months
costs.risk: Buying them back costs 2,415,000 C-bills total; miss the deadline and the carrier sells them

options.title: Offer a share of future earnings and first call on your transport
advantages: No real cash down beyond 200,000 in good faith, so the war chest stays intact
Carriers live on steady freight, and a mercenary unit's regular business is genuinely valuable to the right captain
Builds a relationship that outlasts the crisis — reliable transport without owning any
disadvantages: 8 percent of your next two contracts is real money, paid from earnings you have not made yet
The captain may just refuse: a promise from a unit that just lost its employer is worth less
Working out this unusual deal takes 1 to 2 days the fighter timeline may not give you
options.consequence: If he agrees, you lift owing your next two paydays a cut and the carrier a debt of honor. If he refuses, you have burned the clock and the lien is your only door left.

costs.resource: 8 percent of your next 2 contracts, plus the carrier gets first call on all your transport for 24 months
costs.risk: If he refuses after a day of talks, only the lien is left — now on his stronger terms

entries.event: Surrender broadcast; your contract voids; militia begin seizing infrastructure, including the Gap toll forts.
All three Gap chokepoints confirmed under militia control; flags changed, tolls not yet set.
{TARGET_FACTION} scouts reach the plateau edge; the envoy's truce offer formally opens and the clock on it starts.
Enemy fighters begin scouting the port approaches; the carrier captain starts holding your delay against you.
The enemy regiment is expected at the Gap's east mouth; the route starts closing.
Enemy fighters expected to seal the port; the carrier begins final loading no matter who has arrived.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The carrier lifts at T+10 days, midnight port time, with whoever and whatever is aboard and paid for. After that, the only way off {WORLD} is the enemy's mercy — which the surrender terms do not extend to bandits.

opforSketch.composition: Pursuit: {TARGET_FACTION} regimental combat group — 2 'Mech battalions (regular, one veteran company), armor and mechanized infantry support, limited aerospace tasked primarily to the port. Chokepoints: militia garrisons of 30-60 with crew-served weapons; fort two adds 2 dug-in armored vehicles. Quality: pursuit regulars are disciplined; militia are opportunists with mortgages.
opforSketch.behavior: The pursuit commander wants the iron intact and the precedent set — expect maneuver to block the Gap's east mouth rather than destruction for its own sake, with escalating patience once the column is classified bandit. Militia at the forts fight only when cornered or when the column looks beatable; money moves them faster than threats.

forks.name: OPERATION SOLVENT GHOST
forks.trigger: Column off-world with 75+ percent of equipment; the dead government's off-world escrow located
forks.consequence: The unit's final 4,200,000 in unpaid fees sits in a {TARGET_FACTION} prize-court vault on a border world, listed as enemy state assets. Recovering your own pay from a vault that does not know it owes you: there is paper for this, and there is also the other way.

forks.name: OPERATION REMNANT ROAD
forks.trigger: The carrier lifts with the column — or part of it — still on {WORLD}
forks.consequence: Whoever remains is a bandit force by law and a guerrilla force by necessity: stay alive, stay armed, and stay findable by the retrieval that command swears it will arrange, against an occupier consolidating by the week.

forks.name: OPERATION BORROWED IRON
forks.trigger: Personnel extracted but heavy equipment below 50 percent
forks.consequence: A unit of skills without machines takes the only paper on offer: a cadre contract training a minor House's greens, with an option clause to earn salvage title on the training battalion's worn iron. Pride is not a line item; the roster eats.

storyElementSeed: A quartermaster chalks the column order on a barracks door at dawn — recovery vehicles center, water trailers forward — then rubs out the unit crest above it and writes nothing in its place.

resourceGates.appliesTo: Pay in full from the treasury
resourceGates.lackingText: Treasury short of the fee: option renders with the deficit in red and the carrier's bridge note appended — 'the difference can ride as a lien on cargo of my choosing, Captain, or it can stay on the ground; the tide chart is yours to read.'
If the unit owns DropShip capacity, the carrier's leverage halves: fee reprices to 1,100,000 for the jump-charter legs only, and the lien option is struck from the master's printed schedule.

skeleton: an army deep inland must march itself, its dependents, and its capital to the port after its employer ceases to exist mid-contract, weighing a victor's parley that may be cheaper than the chokepoints or may be the knife, while the chartered lift home demands the fee the dead employer was supposed to pay
inspiration: the Ten Thousand's march to the sea after Cunaxa — Xenophon's Anabasis, including the parley that killed the generals

title: OPERATION LATE GAZETTE
situation: The bounty deal was the cleanest contract your unit had signed in years: 75,000 C-bills for each raider 'Mech confirmed destroyed, 120,000 for one captured in working condition, and 400,000 for {NPC:opfor-commander}, the band's leader, alive or clearly identified. {EMPLOYER}'s district government wanted this band — which has hit 9 settlements in 14 months — hunted to destruction. After 11 weeks of tracking, you have them: grounded in the Ashvein Barrens, a 600-square-km field of collapsed lava tubes on {WORLD}'s northern highlands. The rock hides their reactor heat, and a cave mouth on the north face hides something the size of a DropShip. That report is 3 days old and solid, backed by a heat survey and a bribed water hauler. The band has 9 to 14 'Mechs, light and medium, barely kept running, plus crewed support vehicles (that count is 3 days old and rough). You have already earned 3 bounties on the way in — 225,000 C-bills, payable when you deliver the evidence to the district seat. Your costs so far: 210,000. Then, two nights before the strike, {NPC:intel-source} passes you a page from a merchant newssheet, 6 days out of the capital: {EMPLOYER}'s court has signed a full pardon that turns the band into a district militia if they stop raiding. The problem is the date it takes effect. The newssheet says 'upon signature,' and the signing date itself is only secondhand rumor. So your hunting license may have expired 6 days ago, may expire tomorrow, or may not be signed yet. Any fight after that moment is not war — it is murder, the salvage is theft, and your own contract charges you 1.5 times the bounty value for each machine you wrongly engage. No official courier has reached you yet. Under contract law the bounties stay valid until you are formally notified — but a court will later judge what you knew and when. One more twist in the last paragraph: the pardon only covers band members who comply. Any part of the band that keeps raiding loses that protection. The band may not know about the pardon either. They may know and not care. They may split over it — and the splinter that keeps fighting is still worth 75,000 a head, if you can tell the two halves apart through a gun camera at 600 meters.

objectives.primary: End the band as a raiding threat — by destroying them, capturing them, or confirming they have accepted the pardon — without triggering the penalty for a wrongful attack.
objectives.secondary: Deliver your earned bounty evidence (3 confirmed kills, 225,000 C-bills) to the district seat and collect before the legal situation shifts again.
objectives.bonus: Take {NPC:opfor-commander}, the 400,000 C-bill target, in a way that holds up under legal review no matter which rules turn out to have been in force.

complications.name: When the Pardon Took Effect
complications.text: Nobody has confirmed the exact hour the pardon took effect, and all you have is a 6-day-old newssheet. No one has formally notified you, which probably keeps your bounties valid. But a court will later rebuild the timeline using documents you have never seen.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Every fight is time-stamped in the campaign log. When the pardon's effective hour is later fixed (the generator rolls it within a 3-to-7-day window around the newssheet date), any fight after that hour loses its bounty and costs you 1.5x the bounty value for each machine you engaged.

complications.name: Compliance Cuts Both Ways
complications.text: The pardon only protects band members who stop raiding. A group that keeps raiding is lawful prey. But fire on a group that has complied, and you have a lawsuit on your hands. Through a gun camera, the two look like identical machines with identical paint.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Each band element has a hidden status: complied or not. Attacking a complied element triggers the wrongful-attack penalty. Ignoring a non-complied element lets it keep raiding (failing your primary objective). You can only learn a group's status through contact, watching its behavior, or talking to it.

complications.name: Sunk Costs
complications.text: You are 210,000 C-bills into this operation, against 225,000 you have earned. Quit now and you roughly break even. But every extra day in the Barrens is spent chasing bounties that may already be worthless.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The brief shows a running break-even total. Each extra day of operations costs 6,000 to 9,000 C-bills (fuel, rations, vehicle wear). Your projected treasury is recalculated live for every decision-point option.

decisionPoints.name: The Gazette Problem
decisionPoints.context: The strike is staged. The band is grouped together, located, and unaware. The newssheet page is pinned to the ops board with the date circled. A lawyer is 4 days' ride away, and your chance to strike lasts only hours. Whatever you do next, you do without knowing the law for certain.

options.title: Strike now, before anyone can formally notify you
advantages: The band is grouped and surprised — the best tactical position you will ever have against them
The contract keeps your bounties valid until you are formally notified
Maximum payout: the full schedule, including the 400,000 for the leader, is on the table tonight
disadvantages: If the pardon took effect before your strike, you have gunned down pardoned militia in their beds — legally and in public
The penalty could run past 600,000 C-bills, plus murder charges against named MechWarriors
Even a legally clean strike, a week after a public pardon, looks like bounty-hunting against the peace, and the boards remember how it looked, not the fine print
options.consequence: You fight with maximum advantage and maximum legal risk. Once the pardon's effective hour is fixed, it judges your whole operation in hindsight.

costs.risk: A penalty up to 600,000 C-bills plus criminal charges, if the pardon took effect first

options.title: Stand down and check the facts at the district seat
advantages: Legal certainty: ride back with your earned evidence, collect 225,000, and read the actual decree
No penalty risk, and your conduct is clean in any later case
Your earned bounties turn into cash before any clause can change again
disadvantages: 8-day round trip, and the band will scatter long before you return — the camp empties the first time a sentry sees dust
The hunt restarts against a scattered band at 6,000 to 9,000 C-bills per day, with the bounties possibly dead
If the pardon is real, the contract is over and 11 weeks of tracking becomes a paid invoice and nothing more
options.consequence: You trade your tactical advantage for legal safety. The campaign either ends in clean mediocrity or restarts three times harder.

costs.resource: you lose the element of surprise for good; the staged strike cannot be set up again
costs.risk: The band scatters or flies off-world during your trip to check

options.title: Notify the band yourself — send the pardon terms in under a truce flag
advantages: Forces the legal question onto the band: anyone who keeps raiding after being notified is clearly lawful, bounty-valid prey
Casts you as the pardon's enforcer instead of its victim, and the district government owes you for that
Splits the band along its real fault line: the tired ones take the deal, and the hard core reveals itself
disadvantages: It reveals your presence and rough strength, spending your staged strike as surely as if you had launched it
The meeting is a perfect ambush chance for a leader with 400,000 reasons to distrust truce flags
Nothing forces {EMPLOYER} to honor bounties on a band you just tipped off — the lawyers call this untested ground
options.consequence: The band splits on contact with the terms: a complying majority stands down in place, and a smaller, harder splinter — now legally exposed — keeps its guns. The hunt resumes with clean targets but no surprise.

costs.resource: you spend the element of surprise in exchange for being able to tell targets apart
costs.risk: Your meeting party is exposed, and truce flags have failed in these Barrens before

decisionPoints.name: The Splinter's Former Friends
decisionPoints.context: The pardon is confirmed. But a splinter — 4 to 6 'Mechs of the band's hardest core — has rejected it, hit a settlement, and taken 11 hostages back into the lava-tube country. The pardoned majority, now nominally district militia, sends a rider to your camp with an offer: they know every tube, every cache, and every habit of their former comrades, and they will guide your hunt for a one-third cut of the bounties.

options.title: Take the guides, share the bounty
advantages: Nobody alive knows the splinter's hideouts better, so the hunt drops from weeks to days
Speed helps the hostages survive more than anything else does
It binds the pardoned group to the district's side with paid, bloody-handed commitment
disadvantages: A third of the bounties is a real price: roughly 150,000 C-bills at the expected yield
{EMPLOYER}'s paymaster may refuse to pay bounty money to last month's raiders, so expect a payment fight even if you win
Every guide is a former comrade of your prey; one warning whispered down a tube costs you an ambush
options.consequence: The hunt runs fast but compromised: better local knowledge, divided loyalty, and a payment dispute already forming at the district seat.

costs.resource: you give up 33 percent of the bounties to the guides
costs.risk: Guide betrayal is a live threat; any ambush the splinter springs was bought with information from inside your own column

options.title: Refuse — hunt alone, hunt clean
advantages: You keep the full bounty schedule, with no payment dispute and no divided camp
No risk of betrayal from inside your column
Your evidence stays simple for the legal review that is surely coming
disadvantages: The tube country swallows hunters with no guides, so the hunt takes about three times as long
Every day lowers the hostages' odds — 11 names on your conscience and in the district's newssheets
The rejected militia group sits idle, insulted, and armed — a second problem building behind the first
options.consequence: The hunt is slow, honest, and expensive. What it costs in days it may cost in hostages, and the newssheets will do that math in public.

costs.resource: operating cost of 6,000 to 9,000 C-bills per day across a hunt that takes three times as long
costs.risk: Hostages die, the district loses patience, and the idle militia group does something of its own

options.title: Use them at arm's length — blocking positions only, flat fee
advantages: The militia group seals the tube exits it knows without ever riding in your column
A flat 30,000 C-bill fee instead of a bounty share — cheap for what it buys
A compromise the paymaster can accept: no bounty money to ex-raiders, just a security subcontract
disadvantages: Blockers who know the ground better than you can also leave one exit quietly open
Coordinating across a trust gap: no shared radio encryption, no shared fire plan
Slower than full guiding, so you still have to dig the splinter out tube by tube
options.consequence: The blockade is real but leaky in exactly the spots where loyalty failed. The hunt succeeds or fails on which tube you chose to watch yourself.

costs.risk: One exit left unwatched on purpose is all the splinter needs, and you won't know which one until afterward

entries.event: A sentry alarm goes off at the tube camp; the band's radio net goes active on a frequency you have been reading for 9 days.
The first band 'Mechs power up. The tubes hide their heat, so they start warm — assume they can fight from T+3:00.
The band scatters as planned: 3 to 4 groups break out through separate tube exits, and support vehicles abandon anything not already loaded.
The scattered groups meet at backup rally points 40+ km out. Chasing past this line means single-machine hunts in ground they know.
The DropShip on the north face lifts off with whatever has reached it.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: At T+50:00 from the first alarm, the band's DropShip lifts from the north tube mouth with every machine that reached the ramp. After that, the hunt spreads system-wide, and the bounty schedule pays nothing for that.

opforSketch.composition: 9-14 light and medium 'Mechs in raider condition — mismatched armor, ammunition poverty, 2-3 machines down for parts at any given time — plus 6-8 armed support vehicles and a Buccaneer-class DropShip of doubtful annual certification. Quality: green-to-regular pilots, veteran survival instincts. The leader's bodyguard element (3 machines) is the band's only formation that maneuvers as a unit.
opforSketch.behavior: Raiders fight to disengage, always: scatter doctrine on contact, rally at depth, lift if pressed. They will not stand to defend the camp — only the DropShip ramp, where they will stand all the way down. If the amnesty splits them, the compliant element goes passive in place while the splinter inherits the doctrine and the meanest machines.

forks.name: OPERATION QUIET ROAD
forks.trigger: Band resolved without wrongful-engagement liability; district raids ended
forks.consequence: The district offers the unit the standing anti-raid garrison contract the amnesty was supposed to make unnecessary — modest rate, long term, and a militia auxiliary of former raiders on the same roster. Professional. Awkward. Renewable.

forks.name: OPERATION PAID RANSOM
forks.trigger: Splinter element lifts off-world with hostages aboard
forks.consequence: The district's bounty schedule does not cross the atmosphere, but the broadsheets put the unit's name beside 11 hostages, and {EMPLOYER} offers pursuit terms that pay in reputation recovery more than C-bills. Following is optional. Being the outfit that didn't is permanent.

forks.name: OPERATION MAKE WHOLE
forks.trigger: Engagement timestamped after the established effective hour — wrongful engagement against amnestied militia
forks.consequence: The settlement is court-ordered: the unit escorts and delivers reparation aid to the amnestied band's home settlements at its own cost, under district observation, through country where its own gun cameras are the evidence against it.

storyElementSeed: A sergeant pins the gazette page to the ops tent post, circles the date twice in grease pencil, and writes underneath: WHICH HOUR. WHOSE CLOCK.

resourceGates.lackingText: No contractor DropShip in-system: if the band lifts, the contract ends at the atmosphere. The brief prints the T+50:00 deadline in red and appends the charter-broker's quote for pursuit lift — 480,000 C-bills, 9 days out — so the cost of not owning a hull is a number, not a feeling.

skeleton: hunter must close on cornered prey whose legal status is being rewritten by a distant signature, where word of the change travels slower than the engagement clock and every timestamp in the gun camera is either a bounty or a felony
inspiration: privateers after the Treaty of Ghent, 1815 — prizes taken after ratification were returned and the captors held liable

title: OPERATION SOFT CURRENCY
situation: The public-order contract for {WORLD}'s capital was signed in {YEAR} by 'the planetary government,' which back then was one thing. It is now two. The Governor's faction holds the executive tower, the Planetary Bank, and — this is the part that matters — the counters where the local paper money you are paid in gets exchanged for hard currency. Your pay is 240,000 of these local notes a month, set by a payment clause nobody argued over at signing. The Assembly faction holds the port, the food distribution network, and the legislature. Each side claims to be your real employer. Each sends you orders under the same contract number. You police the capital for both, which means for neither. The local notes have lost 40 percent of their value against the C-bill in 60 days (based on the port exchange rate, updated daily). The Bank's exchange counters are the only legal way to convert notes to hard currency, and they open and close based on how neutral the Governor thinks you are being. Three months of your pay — about 720,000 notes — sits in an account that is worth less every morning and is held hostage by a faction your contract forbids you to favor. The ground is the Mintway: a 60-meter-wide grand boulevard running 2.3 km between the executive tower and the Assembly hall. Halfway along stands the Planetary Mint — the building that physically prints your pay — behind an iron fence and 8 Bank guards. Most evenings now, crowds form at both ends: 12,000 to 20,000 at peak (based on police counts, 2 days old and solid). Each crowd is salted with the other faction's paid agitators, and each end of the boulevard is backed by a faction militia battalion that has stayed in barracks so far. Your contract's rules-of-force clause limits you to non-lethal force against civilians; you may only use deadly force against armed, organized fighters. The agitators are experts at standing right on that line. {NPC:employer-contact} carries the Governor's orders; the Assembly's arrive by courier on identical letterhead. This week the Assembly added a sweetener to its courier pouch: an offer to rewrite your whole contract in C-bills at 85 percent of face value, effective the moment you sign. All you have to do to get paid in real money is stop being neutral.

objectives.primary: Hold the Mintway: keep the two crowds apart, keep both militia battalions off the boulevard, and keep the Mint from burning through the whole contract cycle.
objectives.secondary: Keep your neutrality on the record — accept or refuse every order in writing, and log every use of force within the rules-of-force clause — so neither side can win a breach case against you in arbitration.
objectives.bonus: Solve the pay problem: end the cycle with your back pay secured in hard currency or solid collateral, by any means that holds up under legal review.

complications.name: Paid in Falling Paper
complications.text: The local note is losing 8 to 12 percent of its value every month, and each riot night speeds it up. The only legal way to convert it is the Bank's counters, and their hours depend on the Governor's mood. So your treasury shrinks daily, and one faction controls the only tap that can stop the leak.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Your saved and incoming pay loses 8 to 12 percent of its value each month (roll monthly). You can only convert to C-bills while your standing with the Governor's faction is neutral or better. Any action they read as anti-Governor freezes the counters for 30 days.

complications.name: Two Signatures
