complications.text: Both sides send orders under the original contract number, and every order you obey becomes evidence in the other side's breach case against you. These cases are real: both factions have hired MRBC lawyers, on Tharkad and New Avalon.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Each order you accept raises your standing with that faction by 1 and lowers it with the other by 1, and adds one item to the other side's breach case. At 5 items, that side sues to cancel the contract for good — and your pay clause dies with it.

complications.name: Paid Agitators
complications.text: Both factions pay agitators to stand in the other's crowd and stage the incident that lets their militia march in to 'restore order.' The first killing on the Mintway, by anyone, turns both crowds violent and brings both battalions out of barracks.
complications.mechanicalEffect: If you use deadly force against anyone not confirmed as an armed, organized fighter: riot intensity rises one step, both militia battalions move up to staging positions, and a rules-of-force review automatically opens a breach item against you.

decisionPoints.name: The Re-Paper Offer
decisionPoints.context: The Assembly's courier waits for a written answer: C-bills at 85 percent of face value, effective on signature, with all your back pay converted too. The offer is real and the money is real. And {NPC:employer-contact} has already hinted, pleasantly, that the Governor's office knows about the offer and is watching what you do with it.

options.title: Sign the Assembly's contract
advantages: Real money: 85 percent of face in hard currency beats 100 percent of a note that loses a tenth of its value every month
Converting your back pay rescues the 720,000-note account before it halves again
One employer, one set of orders, one set of books — the confusion ends
disadvantages: The Governor declares breach within hours and the Bank freezes all note conversion, so your saved account is stuck and now worthless as leverage
The Governor's militia now sees you as a player, not a referee, and half the capital's crowds agree
Once you sell your neutrality, you can never buy it back
options.consequence: You are solvent but no longer neutral: the Mintway's referee becomes one side's tool, and the other side starts planning around that.

costs.resource: your 720,000-note account is frozen by the Bank; you only get it back through arbitration or the Governor's fall
costs.risk: Your standing with the Governor's faction drops to hostile, and you now police crowds that think you were bought

options.title: Refuse and keep the original contract
advantages: Your neutrality stays intact and on the record, so your arbitration position is spotless
Both sides still need you more than they distrust you, and the referee's seat is the safest chair in the capital
No faction's crowd has a chant about you yet
disadvantages: Your pay keeps dying at 8 to 12 percent a month, compounding, while your support staff's families buy bread in the same failing notes
The Assembly reads your refusal as a quiet lean toward the Governor, and their breach case does not pause for good intentions
Hired technical staff paid in paper start looking like a desertion risk
options.consequence: You stay neutral and get poorer every week you succeed. The pay leak becomes the campaign's quiet countdown.

costs.resource: your treasury loses 8 to 12 percent of its real value each month, compounding
costs.risk: You lose more support staff each month the notes fall, as trained techs take port jobs paid in C-bills

options.title: Counter-offer both sides: a joint C-bill escrow, or you stop work
advantages: An escrow account funded 50/50 in hard currency is the one setup neither side can call taking sides
The threat to stop work is real leverage: neither faction can police the Mintway, and neither wants the other to try
If they agree, your pay problem is solved without spending your neutrality
disadvantages: Forcing two sides who each deny the other exists to co-sign anything takes 7 days of shuttle diplomacy the Mintway may not allow
If either refuses, you have formally threatened to stop work — one item for both breach cases at once
An escrow agent licensed for disputed-ownership accounts charges 4 percent and asks questions in writing
options.consequence: You force both sides to show which one actually wants order in the capital. The answer reshapes the contract or ends it.

costs.risk: If both refuse, you have threatened both paymasters in the same week, with the riot season still coming

decisionPoints.name: The Mint
decisionPoints.context: Riot night, the worst one yet. Both crowds are on the Mintway, both militia battalions stand at their ends pretending to be parade formations, and the Mint's 8 Bank guards have locked the fence and called the executive tower for help. The Governor orders you to garrison the Mint — 'protecting essential government property.' The Assembly's courier demands the Mint be sealed under joint custody until the government dispute is settled. And the building between the two crowds is the one that prints the money you are owed.

options.title: Garrison the Mint under the Governor's order
advantages: Tactically the cleanest: one defensible building, a clear perimeter, and the Bank guards help instead of resist
The Governor's gratitude comes in the form you need: expect your frozen account unfrozen and converted within days
It stops the night's most likely arson target from actually burning
disadvantages: Obeying the Governor's order on the most disputed building is the biggest item yet for the Assembly's breach case
The Assembly crowd sees mercenaries on the Mint fence as the Bank buying an army, so the crowd gets angrier right where you stand
You become the thing the agitators aim at, and your rules-of-force limits get tested in front of 20,000 witnesses
options.consequence: The Mint survives the night; your neutrality does not. The Assembly's lawyers add the item and start drafting their case.

costs.resource: the Assembly breach case gains 2 items (obeying an order on disputed property)
costs.risk: Your people become the main target on the boulevard, where one agitator with a pistol can decide the night

options.title: Seal it under joint custody — observers from both sides, garrisoned by neither
advantages: The one outcome both breach cases struggle to use: you protected the building FROM both sides
Joint observer teams put faction people side by side in one calm room — a small but real step toward peace
It honors the contract's real purpose — public order — over either side's order
disadvantages: You obey neither order, so your standing with both sides drops and both paymasters note the defiance
Joint custody means negotiating observer terms tonight, on the boulevard, through megaphones and couriers
If the seal fails — one fence breach, one fire — you own that failure alone, having claimed the authority alone
options.consequence: The Mint becomes the capital's one jointly-run building: a model for calming things down, or a hostage to the next riot, depending on nights you cannot control.

costs.resource: your standing with both factions drops by 1 (you defied both orders)
costs.risk: You alone own any custody failure, and the negotiation happens inside the riot itself

options.title: Hold it yourself — assert a wage lien on the Mint as collateral
advantages: The contract's lien clause (standard MRBC boilerplate nobody reads) arguably lets you seize collateral for 720,000 notes of unpaid real value
Whoever holds the Mint has the leverage to force the escrow talks both sides have dodged
Your pay stops being a hostage and becomes your hostage instead
disadvantages: Both sides will call it seizure of government property by a foreign armed force — because that is roughly what it is
The lien only holds up in review if your rules-of-force record is spotless and the seizure is bloodless; one casualty makes it armed robbery
Holding a building both militias want is an open invitation to a siege, written in your own hand
options.consequence: The boldest move in your history: the pay dispute becomes a fortified position, and both sides must now negotiate with their referee — or break it.

costs.resource: your standing with both factions drops by 2, and both breach cases gain 1 item
costs.risk: The lien only holds up if the seizure is bloodless; one casualty makes it armed robbery of government property. Holding the building also invites a siege by both militias.

entries.event: Evening crowds converge on the Mintway from both ends; police counts pass 12,000 and their commanders go home.
An agitator strikes — the likely flashpoint is a firebomb thrown at the Mint fence, with the thrower impossible to identify.
The Governor's militia battalion forms up in the executive tower courtyard, 'just to be ready.'
The Assembly's militia battalion forms up on the legislature steps, citing the other side's move.
If the Mint fence is breached: fires reach the printing halls in about 35 minutes, and everyone's pay burns together.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: If both militia battalions step onto the Mintway while the crowds are still between them, the contract — every version of it — voids at H+3:00 because open civil war has broken out. Keep the battalions off the boulevard, or the riot turns into a battle nobody hired you to fight.

opforSketch.composition: Crowds of 12,000-20,000 with 30-60 paid agitators per side; about 8-12 people per crowd are armed with firearms (estimated from confiscation rates). Faction militia battalions: 400-500 each, infantry with light vehicles, plus 1 platoon of aging second-line 'Mechs apiece (3-4 machines). Quality: militia regulars with parade-ground polish and no street experience.
opforSketch.behavior: Crowds surge and pull back on 20-40 minute rumor cycles. The agitators work the edge of your rules-of-force limits on purpose: their job is to get wounded by you on camera. The militia battalions advance only behind an incident that justifies it — but each commander thinks the other is about to stage one, which is its own countdown.

forks.name: OPERATION HARD MONEY
forks.trigger: Cycle completed: Mintway held, neutrality documented, joint escrow or equivalent achieved
forks.consequence: Both claimants, unable to fault the referee, jointly contract the unit to guard the Mint and the escrow under dual seal — the capital's only institution both sides trust, paid at last in C-bills, resented at last by everyone.

forks.name: OPERATION PAPER ASHES
forks.trigger: Militia battalions meet on the Mintway; contract voids by supervening civil conflict
forks.consequence: The capital is a two-army city and the unit's cantonment — with its dependents, its workshops, and its worthless beautiful banknotes — sits between the armies. Getting the unit's own out through a city at war is the contract now, and nobody is paying for it.

forks.name: OPERATION COMPANY SCRIP
forks.trigger: Unit read as partisan (re-paper signed, or Governor tasking honored on the Mint, with breach filed)
forks.consequence: The claimant that owns the unit now garrisons it at its own strongpoints, paid in promises against victory, while the other claimant's counsel pursues the breach case across every hiring board the unit ever hopes to use again.

storyElementSeed: A paymaster counts the month's notes into even stacks, then weighs the stacks on a parts scale and logs the weight instead of the count.

is-steiner.decisionPoints[0].context: The Assembly's courier waits for a written answer, and the offer is drafted the Lyran way — exchange-rate tables, conversion schedules, a footnote on archival precedent from three other contested worlds. C-bills at 85 percent of face. The covering letter regrets the circumstances and quotes commercial law. {NPC:employer-contact} has already mentioned, between pleasantries, that the Governor's office holds the unit's redemption schedule and reviews it weekly.

is-davion.decisionPoints[0].context: The Assembly's courier waits for a written answer. The offer is one page: C-bills at 85 percent of face, effective on signature, back-pay included. 'Your people fight better paid in money than in promises — so do ours.' {NPC:employer-contact} has already noted, without quite saying it, that the Governor's office knows the offer exists and that redemption counters have hours.

resourceGates.appliesTo: Hold it yourself — assert a wage lien on the Mint as collateral
resourceGates.lackingText: Without a defensible cantonment inside the capital, a lien garrison at the Mint cannot be relieved, resupplied, or reinforced. The option renders locked, with the line: 'collateral you cannot hold is a gift you have not yet delivered.'

skeleton: a neutral order-keeping force must hold the line between two claimant crowds while its wages are denominated in one claimant's collapsing currency — every act of neutrality is priced against its own payroll, and the building that prints the pay is the flashpoint
inspiration: the Shanghai Volunteer Corps holding the International Settlement through the 1927 crisis, crossed with the Continental scrip collapse — 'not worth a Continental'

title: OPERATION SHORT WEIGHT
situation: The contract sounds simple: 1,800 C-bills per ton of relief cargo delivered to the upland communities of {WORLD}'s {DISTRICT} plateau, with a quota of 4,000 tons in 60 days. {EMPLOYER}'s provincial government wrote it this way because the {TARGET_FACTION} raiding season burned the lowland harvest stores in the same quarter a crop blight ruined the plateau's own harvest — and because paying per ton puts all the risk on you, the contractor. The route is the real problem: the Saltlick Corridor, 340 km of raised causeway across salt flats, one graded lane, two passing sidings, and every convoy visible for 20 km through the heat shimmer. Your fleet is fixed: 28 cargo trucks at 8 tons each, plus your escort and recovery vehicles. The threat is {TARGET_FACTION}-backed irregulars — 2 to 4 light 'Mechs and 8 to 15 armed trucks working from beyond the flats (that report is 5 days old and rough) — plus a growing number of hijack crews who were farmers in the spring. They hit full convoys and let empty ones pass, having done the same math the contract does. Thirty-one days in, with 1,900 tons delivered and the schedule barely holding, the government runs out of money. An apologetic courier notice arrives: cash payments are suspended, and the contract's pay-in-goods clause kicks in. From now on you are paid in grain and fuel, valued by the government's own assessor at 140 percent of market price. But the port's posted prices, 3 days old, tell the real story. The grain is real — the problem is that your wage-grain rides the same 28 trucks as the relief-grain, along the same causeway, past the same communities. Every ton you take as pay is a ton short of your quota, makes the convoy fatter and more tempting to raiders, and rolls slowly past settlements that count axles from the roadside and know to the sack what they were promised. {NPC:employer-contact} signs the shipping manifests. {NPC:intel-source}, a clerk at the upland farmers' co-op, has been your best ambush-warning source for a month — and those warnings track exactly with how the co-op feels about you that week. The contract's delivery clause names 9 communities to receive grain. It says nothing about the tenth.

objectives.primary: Deliver the remaining 2,100 tons to the 9 listed communities inside the 60-day window, losing less than 10 percent of the tonnage to raids.
objectives.secondary: Keep the locals on your side: the co-op's warning network is the difference between ambushes you meet ready and ambushes you walk into.
objectives.bonus: End the contract with your wages turned into something that lasts — hard currency, transport traded for goods, or the corridor toll rights — instead of grain rotting in a warehouse you do not own.

complications.name: The Grain Is Worth Less Than It Says
complications.text: The assessor values your wage-grain at 140 percent of market price for payment. But if you sell it here in a famine, you get only 60 percent — the buyers have no money. So your pay is real tonnage worth half what it says on paper, unless you ship it off-world or turn it into something else.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Pay-in-goods credits are worth 0.6x their stated value if you sell them locally, 1.1x if you ship them off-world (needs transport; see resourceGates), or full value only if converted through DP 'How to Take the Wage,' option 3.

complications.name: The Same Trucks
complications.text: Twenty-eight trucks is your whole fleet. There is no second fleet, no rail line, and the causeway allows no detour. Your wage-grain and the relief-grain compete for the same trucks, in the same convoys, on the same exposed lane.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Each convoy carries up to 224 tons. Tonnage you take as wages counts zero toward the 2,100-ton quota and makes that convoy one step more attractive to raiders for every 40 tons of wage-grain aboard.

complications.name: Hungry Eyes
complications.text: The people by the road are counting. Every community logs each convoy's axle count and direction, and the co-op's warning network is run by people whose children eat or starve based on how you split the load. Hauling your wages is legal and in the contract — and watched.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Any convoy carrying more than 25 percent wage-grain lowers your standing with the locals by 1. Below 0, the ambush warnings stop. Below -2, roadside watchers start reporting your convoy loads to the raiders instead.

decisionPoints.name: How to Take the Wage
decisionPoints.context: The pay-in-goods notice sits on the table next to the quota ledger. You are owed 31 days of work already, and will be owed 29 more. The assessor's rates are generous, but they are paid in a currency that is heavy, edible, and riding on your only trucks. Your lawyer's note in the margin: 'all three options are legal — price them out.'

options.title: Take the grain at assessment, haul it on the quota trucks
advantages: Paid now, in something whose famine-year value is real and rising
No risk of an unpaid debt: the grain exists, unlike the government's cash
The 140 percent rate is, on paper, a raise
disadvantages: Every ton of pay is a ton short of quota, so your objective and your payroll are now the same limited number
Fat convoys draw raiders the way the flats draw heat shimmer
The roadside watches you haul your pay past their hunger at 30 km/h, and that goodwill was your cheap early warning — this spends it
options.consequence: You are rich in grain but short on quota, friends, and warning time. The contract's three clocks now work against each other.

costs.resource: you lose 1 ton of quota capacity per ton of wages hauled, and your standing with the locals is at risk (see Hungry Eyes)
costs.risk: Each wage-laden convoy is more attractive to raiders, and the ambush rate rises with it

options.title: Defer your wages — take a legal claim, get C-bills within 180 days
advantages: Every truck stays on quota, so your schedule and your standing with the locals both survive
A registered MRBC claim against the provincial government is enforceable and jumps the line
Your restraint in a famine is the kind of thing hiring halls hear about
disadvantages: The government that just went broke is the one you are trusting to pay you later
You float your own costs for 180 days — fuel, parts, and pay advances all come from your reserves
If {EMPLOYER}'s government falls or is replaced, your claim waits behind every other creditor of a dead government
options.consequence: The mission stays clean and you become your employer's creditor — a position worth exactly as much as a provincial government's odds of surviving.

costs.resource: your reserves cover 60-90 days of operating costs with no reimbursement
costs.risk: The debtor may default; the claim is only as good as the government that survives the famine it caused

options.title: Take the corridor toll rights instead
advantages: The government offers 7 years of toll income from the rebuilt corridor instead of wages — an asset, not a one-time payout
Expected to pay 2 to 3 times your owed wages if the corridor reopens to commercial traffic
Turns you from creditor to owner: now the raiders are attacking your own income
disadvantages: Toll income needs a corridor at peace, so the rights are worth zero until the raiding ends — meaning your pay now depends on winning
Collecting tolls means staying: a garrison commitment after the contract, on a world you had no plans to keep
A mercenary unit holding a planet's main road for profit is a political target the {DISTRICT} newssheets will name within a month
options.consequence: Your pay becomes a piece of the planet — a long-term investment with a garrison attached, and a reason to care about {WORLD} for years.

costs.resource: a garrison commitment after the contract: at least 1 company on-world to run the toll rights
costs.risk: The rights are worth nothing until the raiding ends; if the raiders win the corridor, you were paid in nothing

decisionPoints.name: The Tenth Community
decisionPoints.context: Verrun's Forge is not on the delivery list. Its 1,400 people ended up on the losing side of a provincial assembly vote over the spring levy, and the people who drew up the delivery schedule remember that. Their headman walks 31 km to the siding to tell you they are eating their seed grain and boiling leather. Diverting 200 tons feeds them through the gap — but the contract only pays quota credit for the 9 listed communities. {NPC:employer-contact} signs the manifests and is nobody's fool.

options.title: Divert the 200 tons — feed them and take the contract hit
advantages: 1,400 people eat, and your name on this world becomes more than a line on a manifest
The co-op network — Verrun's Forge has family in every listed community — pays you back in warnings what it cannot pay in grain
It is the right thing, and units that always value that at zero end up as outfits nobody quite trusts
disadvantages: 200 tons of delivery you are not paid or credited for: roughly 360,000 C-bills of work the contract will not recognize
A documented breach of the delivery clause gives the government leverage in every future dispute, including your wage claim
{NPC:employer-contact} has to either falsify the manifest or report it, and both are debts someone collects later
options.consequence: Your quota gap grows by 200 tons, but your standing on the plateau hardens into loyalty. The government's books and the roadside's books now disagree about who you are.

costs.resource: you lose 200 tons of uncredited quota, and a contract-breach item goes on file
costs.risk: The government gains leverage in all later disputes, which weakens your position on the bonus objective

options.title: Refuse — the contract is the contract
advantages: Your quota math holds, and the 9 listed communities get every contracted ton on schedule
No breach, no leverage given up, no faked manifest
The government's priority list was always political, and you declining to redraw it is just the contract working as written
disadvantages: Verrun's Forge starves in plain sight, 31 km from a grain convoy, and the plateau knows whose trucks rolled past
The co-op's warning network goes quiet — not hostile at first, just quiet, which on the causeway is the same thing
Hungry communities with nothing to lose are where hijack crews come from, and you may meet Verrun's Forge again, armed
options.consequence: The contract stays clean, and the corridor gets more dangerous by exactly the amount of goodwill this cost you.

costs.resource: your standing with the locals drops by 2, and the ambush-warning channel weakens
costs.risk: New hijack recruits from the unlisted community, and the locals turn against you for the rest of the contract

options.title: Get the list changed — push the official to add Verrun's Forge
advantages: If Verrun's Forge is added, the 200 tons earn full quota credit and full per-ton pay: fed people AND clean books
A changed list sets a precedent — the next unlisted village is a paperwork question, not a moral one
It costs the government almost nothing real; famine relief lists get amended on Tharkad and Luthien alike when officials are reminded who is watching
disadvantages: The change moves at courier speed: 6 to 9 days through the provincial office while the seed grain runs out
{NPC:employer-contact} will want something for pushing it: the going rate for a rush is a 15,000 C-bill 'processing fee' that appears on no schedule
If the assembly faction that dropped Verrun's Forge blocks it, you have spent days and a bribe to be told no in writing
options.consequence: The list becomes the battlefield: paperwork crawls while people boil leather, and the outcome decides whether you can steer the contract or only obey it.

costs.risk: The change may be refused after the delay, and Verrun's Forge gets worse during the paperwork

entries.event: The lead truck hits a buried charge at km 210, 14 km past siding 2, and the convoy stops on the causeway.
Armed trucks appear out of the heat shimmer east of the flats — they were hidden in it the whole time.
The raider light 'Mechs (2-3) commit only if your escort has split off to chase trucks; they will not take on a formed-up escort.
If the convoy is still stopped: a second raider group starts stripping trailers from the rear while the first holds your escort's attention.
Nightfall on the flats. The raiders' night sights are better than yours, and everyone knows it.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: A convoy still stopped on the causeway at nightfall — H+6:40 from the morning siding — is a total loss. The contract's insurance clause won't cover night recovery on an unsecured route. Clear the lane and roll by dusk, or the cargo, the trucks, and the quota credit are all gone by morning.

opforSketch.composition: Sponsored irregulars: 2-4 light 'Mechs (20-35 tons, maintained to raider standard) and 8-15 armed trucks and technicals with crew-served weapons; behind them, a {TARGET_FACTION} sponsor providing fuel and ammunition but no fingerprints. Local hijack crews: unarmored, desperate, growing. Quality: green-to-regular; the 'Mech element is the only disciplined formation.
opforSketch.behavior: Heat-shimmer ambush doctrine: hull-down in the mirage bands, initiate with mines or cut-charges, strip cargo fast, vanish beyond the flats. They preferentially engage the fullest convoy third and avoid formed escorts entirely — their sponsor pays for grain denied, not for battles fought. Hijack crews follow the irregulars like gulls follow a trawler.

forks.name: OPERATION TOLL GATE
forks.trigger: Quota met and the toll concession taken as wages
forks.consequence: The unit now owns 7 years of revenue on a corridor the raiders' sponsor still wants closed. The garrison company the concession requires becomes the contract that never ends — the unit defending its own pay, in place, through the next raid season.

forks.name: OPERATION GLEANING
forks.trigger: Quota missed by 15+ percent; plateau communities enter hard ration
forks.consequence: The shortfall arrives as arithmetic, then as crowds. The administration orders the unit — still its contractor, still on-world, still owed — onto the depot gates against the hungry, and the roadside that counted axles all season remembers exactly whose trucks were short.

forks.name: OPERATION DRY HARVEST
forks.trigger: The raiders' base of operations beyond the flats is fixed by the co-op's warning network
forks.consequence: The administration offers a separate strike contract against the irregulars' staging ground — payable, with what passes for humor in a provincial treasury, partly in kind. The corridor cannot be safe until somebody goes out past the shimmer.

storyElementSeed: A driver chalks two numbers on the tailgate before rolling — tons for them, tons for us — and a child at the first checkpoint reads both aloud, twice, to be sure.

resourceGates.appliesTo: Take the grain at assessment, haul it on the quota trucks
resourceGates.lackingText: No lift capacity off-world: wage-grain assessed at 140 percent of market realizes 60 percent at famine resale. The brief prints both numbers side by side, and the difference is the price of not owning a hull.

skeleton: escort must meet a per-ton relief quota when its own wages are paid in the cargo itself — every ton of pay loaded displaces a ton of quota, fattens the convoy the raiders prefer, and rolls past the people the mission exists to feed
inspiration: Berlin Airlift civil charter carriers — paid by the delivered ton while corridor rules and weather set the arithmetic

title: OPERATION DIVIDED STANDARD
situation: The counter-landing on {WORLD} is the biggest operation {EMPLOYER} has run since the invasion stalled, and your battalion is in the first wave because the pay was real: 2,400,000 C-bills base, a 300,000 cooperation bonus, and command rights at the Liaison level — meaning you take the employer's orders but keep tactical control of your own unit, a step down from full independence, priced accordingly. The target is the Hadrach Shelf: a 14-km coastal terrace under a cliff, the only ground on the continent flat enough to land a regiment and close enough to flank the {TARGET_FACTION} garrison's inland fortress. Four ramp roads climb the cliff. The defenders are a {TARGET_FACTION} garrison cluster at two-thirds strength, with its command star (5 of its best 'Mechs) anchoring ramp 3, the steepest and most important. That report is 8 days old: solid from orbital survey, but only rough on exactly how the command star is positioned. The assault plan, drawn up by {NPC:employer-contact}'s staff, sends three House battalions up ramps 1, 2, and 4 in sequence. Those battalions are 50 to 70 percent green — the flood of new academy graduates since the invasion, brave but untested (from the employer's own readiness reports, shared with you). Then, at H-36, the operations order arrives with paragraph 9. Under contract clause 14 — 'attachment of the unit or parts of it as operational need requires' — your battalion is to be broken into companies and parceled out, one company to stiffen each green battalion, effective on landing. The phrase 'parts of it' was slipped into the employer's final draft and initialed at signing by a major who has since left the unit. Your own analysts ran the numbers twice. Scattered as single companies under green House command, against a Clan cluster fighting on ground it chose, you project 40 percent casualties and the loss of your unit's cohesion — the very thing that makes you worth hiring. Kept together, your battalion projects taking ramp 3 itself — the hardest ramp, the one the plan quietly avoids — at 30 percent casualties, all under your own command. The Liaison channel is open. The landing clock cannot be moved. Once taken, the shelf sits under Clan artillery and fighters until the cliff crest falls — and read the contract again: it bills a fighting evacuation to you, the contractor.

objectives.primary: Take and hold the cliff crest above the Hadrach Shelf by H+36:00, before the {TARGET_FACTION} inland cluster finishes its road march.
objectives.secondary: Keep the battalion whole — its cohesion, its chain of command, and a casualty count that leaves you a unit worth hiring on H+37.
objectives.bonus: Take ramp 3's defended crest with your own command still intact — the ramp the plan avoids, and the one that decides whether the flanking position exists at all.

complications.name: The Attachment Clause
complications.text: Clause 14 lets the employer attach 'the unit or parts of it' as operational need requires. Your lawyer reads 'parts' as limited by the command-integrity rider elsewhere in the contract; the employer's lawyer reads it as the right to split you down to companies. Both readings were initialed by people rushing to meet a deadline.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The order to split up looks legal on its face. To fight it, you must file a formal protest (DP 'Elements Thereof,' option 2) and pay its costs. Defying it without a protest is a documented breach: it voids your cooperation bonus and hands the employer a counterclaim.

complications.name: Green Stiffening
complications.text: The three House battalions are 50 to 70 percent first-combat troops. They are not cowards, just new — and a Clan garrison cluster is a brutal first teacher. A company of yours attached to a green battalion is stuck with its host's reactions at every moment that matters.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Any of your companies operating split off under a green host battalion uses the host's morale and fire-discipline ratings in combat. When the host fails a check, your attached company suffers too: forced retreats, blocked fire lanes, and abandoned flanks.

complications.name: The Shelf Clock
complications.text: Until the crest falls, the shelf is a target the Clan artillery and fighters hit on their own schedule. Your grounded DropShips, your supplies, and the field hospital sit on that beach the whole time.
complications.mechanicalEffect: For each 12 hours the crest stays contested: 2 percent of your landed supplies are destroyed (adding up), one hazard roll hits a grounded DropShip, and the medical backlog grows — moving the wounded competes with moving ammunition on the same ramps.

decisionPoints.name: Elements Thereof
decisionPoints.context: H-36. Paragraph 9 sits between your contract and your casualty projection. The employer's Liaison expects your acknowledgment by H-30. Three ways to read one clause, three ways down to the shelf, and the only thing beyond dispute is that the landing happens no matter what.

options.title: Obey — split into companies as ordered
advantages: Your cooperation bonus (300,000 C-bills) and your employer relationship both survive intact
The green battalions genuinely fight better with veteran companies alongside — the stiffening logic is not wrong, just paid for in other people's blood
No protest, no breach risk, no arbitration hanging over your next decade
disadvantages: A projected 40 percent casualties, spread out where your own command cannot reach them
Your unit's cohesion — the thing hiring halls actually pay for — is spent into three formations that will not remember the cost
Every one of your company commanders fights under a green battalion staff making its first real decisions against a Clan cluster
options.consequence: You perform as contracted and bleed as projected. Whatever walks off the shelf carries your name on a roster that took years to build and one operation to spend.

costs.resource: a projected 40 percent casualties across your scattered companies, and your cohesion rating drops one step no matter the outcome
costs.risk: Company-level disasters under green host command are charged to your record, not the hosts'

options.title: Formal protest — invoke the command-integrity rider and demand liaison review
advantages: The rider's wording is genuinely on your side; a neutral reading favors keeping the battalion whole
The protest protects every legal position: your bonus, your breach defense, and the arbitration record for later
If it succeeds, your battalion fights together with clean paper behind it
disadvantages: The review costs the assault a day of your weight: the first wave lands without your battalion while the judges read
If the green battalions crack on day one, being right will not be the same as being forgiven — by the employer or by the survivors
If the review sides with the employer (the clause is honestly unclear), you are back to obey-or-breach with the relationship already burned
options.consequence: The landing goes in a battalion short while the paperwork fight runs. The outcome — and what happened on the ramps during it — defines your reputation both ways at once.

costs.resource: your battalion is held out of the first wave during the review
costs.risk: Day-one assault results happen without you, and your employer relations drop by 1 win or lose

options.title: Counter-propose: your battalion takes ramp 3, whole
advantages: You stay whole AND the general gains a ramp the plan had given up on — the operational need met by a better offer
30 percent projected casualties, but under your own command, with your own recovery and medical practices
If it works, 'the battalion that took ramp 3' is the line every hiring hall reads for ten years
disadvantages: Ramp 3 is anchored by the command star: the hardest fight on the continent, and you volunteered for it
A counter-proposal that gets rejected is a protest made without the protest's legal protections
You now owe the plan a win: if ramp 3 stalls, you proved the split-up order right in front of everyone
options.consequence: The general accepts — a whole battalion against the worst objective costs the plan nothing — and you have bought your integrity at the price of the command star's full attention.

costs.resource: a projected 30 percent casualties, all on your own roster, plus double the normal ammunition load
costs.risk: The objective is rated EXTREME; failure turns your integrity argument into the employer's example of what not to do

decisionPoints.name: The Recall That Is Not One
decisionPoints.context: H+19. Your battalion is two-thirds up ramp 3, with the command star giving ground by meters, when a lawful order comes over the Liaison channel: break off, come down, and reinforce the green battalion collapsing on ramp 1. Obeying means giving up ground you won, your casualty collection point, and the momentum that is the only thing cheaper than blood on a cliff. Refusing is documented disobedience of a lawful order, mid-assault, on the record.

options.title: Comply in full — break off and come down
advantages: You obey a lawful order on the record, so your bonus and legal position stay intact
Ramp 1's collapse genuinely threatens the whole shelf — the order is not stupid, just expensive for you
The green battalion you save remembers, and so does its parent regiment, which votes on hiring for a generation
disadvantages: You give up the ground you won on ramp 3 with your casualty collection point still forward — wounded and salvage left under Clan guns
The command star re-anchors, so ramp 3 will cost full price again if anyone climbs it later
Your battalion arrives at ramp 1 tired, depleted, and angry — stiffening in a worse mood than this morning
options.consequence: The shelf is probably saved and the crest probably not taken by deadline. The operation grinds toward the fighting-evacuation clause everyone has now read twice.

costs.resource: you give up your ramp 3 gains, leaving your forward casualty collection point and battlefield salvage under Clan control
costs.risk: The crest-by-H+36 objective is in jeopardy, and the Shelf Clock keeps costing you

options.title: Split the difference — send one company down, push the crest with two
advantages: Ramp 1 gets real help within the hour, and ramp 3 keeps some of its momentum
The least-bad math if both fights can be won — and your own analysts say they can, narrowly
You keep your forward casualty collection point and salvage line
disadvantages: Partly obeying a full order is legally the worst spot to be in — neither obedience nor principled refusal — and the judge will say so
Two companies against the command star is the thin edge of the original projection
If either fight fails, the finding will blame your split, not the order or the cluster
options.consequence: You bet you can be right twice at once, balancing the legal risk of disobeying against the tactical risk of obeying.

costs.resource: you break up your force at the decisive point: 2 companies against the command star
costs.risk: Partial-compliance breach: the employer can void your cooperation bonus, and both fights run at a reduced margin

options.title: Refuse, citing the rider — finish ramp 3 fast and swing from the crest
advantages: The crest, once taken, unhinges every ramp: the fastest real help ramp 1 can get is a flanked cluster
You fight your own plan to your own finish — the integrity argument carried to its honest end
If the timing holds, the refusal becomes a footnote to a victory, and history is kind to crests taken
disadvantages: Documented refusal of a lawful order, mid-assault: breach, forfeited bonus, and an MRBC conduct file no matter the outcome
Ramp 1 collapses or holds on its own during the hours the swing takes — and you chose that for them
If ramp 3 stalls even briefly, you have disobeyed your way straight into the disaster the order predicted
options.consequence: Everything rides on the summit clock: you are either the battalion that won the battle by refusing an order, or the one that lost the shelf the same way — and the arbitration panel reads the same gun-camera either way.

costs.resource: you forfeit the cooperation bonus (300,000 C-bills) on refusal, no matter the outcome
costs.risk: Employer relations drop by 3, an MRBC conduct file opens, and your standing recovers only if the assault succeeds

entries.event: The first wave lands on the Hadrach Shelf. The Clan garrison acknowledges the landing on an open channel — formal, unhurried, already ranging its guns.
First fighter strike on the beach: DropShip point defenses engage, and you start dispersing supplies under fire.
A trinary counterattacks at the base of ramp 2 — the cluster tests the greenest formation first, and finds it wanting.
The command star is confirmed moving to the ramp 3 crest, and the artillery finishes ranging the shelf.
A second trinary arrives from the inland fortress; the defense is now at full garrison strength.
The inland cluster's road march is reported at the halfway point (that report is 2 hours old and solid, from aerial recon).

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: You must hold the cliff crest by H+36:00, when the inland cluster finishes its march. If the shelf is still contested at H+36, you face a fighting evacuation — and the contract bills fighting evacuations to you, the contractor, including any damage to your ships.

opforSketch.composition: {TARGET_FACTION} garrison cluster at two-thirds strength: 2 trinaries of second-line OmniMechs plus a front-line command star (5 machines, veteran-to-elite), Elemental support, 1 artillery battery on the crest plateau, and 2 fighter pairs cycling from the inland fortress. Inland: a second cluster on a road march, arriving H+36. This report is 8 days old, updated by aerial recon, and solid.
opforSketch.behavior: The cluster fights to hold ground: it gives up nothing and counterattacks wherever a ramp assault loses its formation. On ramp 3 the command star fights by zellbrigen — the Clan honor code of one-on-one duels — unless the attacker fights dishonorably, which frees it to gang up. That code favors a disciplined attacker and punishes a ragged one. Artillery hits the shelf on a steady rhythm, and fighters hunt anything moving between ramps.

forks.name: OPERATION HIGH WATER MARK
forks.trigger: Crest taken by H+36; the inland cluster declines battle and withdraws to the keep
forks.consequence: The unit garrisons the sector it bled for through the counter-raid season, on a renewal whose rate finally reflects the casualty sheet — and with a Clan keep forty kilometers inland that has not finished the conversation.

forks.name: OPERATION SHELF TIDE
forks.trigger: Crest contested at H+36; the inland cluster reaches the escarpment
forks.consequence: Contested evacuation under the annex that bills it to the contractor: lifting wounded, machines, and stores off a beach under artillery while the employer's staff drafts the after-action that explains whose fault the arithmetic was.

forks.name: OPERATION LOUD FLANK
forks.trigger: Crest half-taken; operations staff needs the cluster's attention held while House regulars regroup
forks.consequence: The unit — relations strained, bonus disputed, still the best formation on the shelf — is tasked to mount a loud, sustained feint along the escarpment's far shoulder. The order does not use the word expendable. It does not have to.

storyElementSeed: A company sergeant repaints the battalion number on a borrowed fender, stops halfway through the second digit, and stands there with the brush, deciding which number is true tonight.

is-davion.decisionPoints[0].context: H-36. Paragraph 9 sits on the command couch between the contract and the casualty projection. The liaison's covering note is pure New Avalon staff school: 'Stiffening assignments per clause 14. Acknowledge by H-30. Your people are professionals; that's why we're spending them this way.' The landing happens regardless.

is-kurita.decisionPoints[0].context: H-36. Paragraph 9 sits on the command couch between the contract and the casualty projection. The liaison's covering note invokes duty the way Luthien drafts it: 'The Coordinator's soldiers and your own will share one fate on the ramps. Clause 14 merely names what honor already requires. Acknowledge by H-30.' The landing happens regardless.

is-steiner.decisionPoints[0].context: H-36. Paragraph 9 sits on the command couch between the contract and the casualty projection. The liaison's covering note arrives with annexes of its own: 'Attachment schedule per clause 14, with revised logistics tables. The Estates-General expects economy of force; your battalion's distribution achieves a 12 percent efficiency. Acknowledge by H-30.' The landing happens regardless.

green_fraction.unit: percent first-combat personnel in House battalions

resourceGates.appliesTo: Formal protest — invoke the command-integrity rider and demand liaison review
resourceGates.lackingText: Priority ComStar transmission to the MRBC field office is 40,000 C-bills the treasury does not hold: the protest rides a courier boat instead, 4 days each way. The brief prints the courier timeline beside the assault timeline so the gap can be read as what it is.

skeleton: an attached battalion must keep itself whole through someone else's assault plan, when the employer's clause arguably allows dissolving it into stiffeners for green formations — the integrity of the force is itself the contract object in dispute, and the order that would spend it is lawful
inspiration: the AEF amalgamation crisis, 1917-18 — allied commands demanding American battalions be fed piecemeal into foreign divisions, and the refusal that kept the army whole

title: OPERATION COURTESY CALL
situation: For 7 months the {DISTRICT} industrial complex on {WORLD} has run on an arrangement nobody wrote down: two mercenary outfits, two employers, one working prize. Your unit holds the south half — the fusion-turbine plant and the rolling mills — under contract to the corporate board that backed {EMPLOYER}'s claimant. The north half — the fabrication halls and the foundry furnaces — belongs to a rival outfit of 2 companies (20-24 'Mechs, regular-to-veteran, kept to a standard you privately respect) under contract to the regional duke's government, which backed the other side. Between the two halves runs the Common Spur: 5.6 km of rail line both contracts require you to keep working. You and the rivals share scheduled time slots on it under a safety agreement the two commands wrote themselves across a table in a freight office — the Greenline Memorandum, signed by neither employer, honored by both outfits, and the reason the complex still runs. The rivalry has been real but professional: poached techs, undercut renewal bids, a standing bet on whose half ships more tonnage. Both outfits want the same thing — the single whole-complex contract that goes to whoever is left when the war picks a winner. Eleven days ago the war picked. The duke's government was outlawed, the rival outfit's contract was voided automatically, and their pay stopped — 5 weeks of back pay owed and counting (their own quartermaster told yours over drinks; the report is 2 days old and solid). They hold the north half anyway. Their price to leave: a 480,000 C-bill exit payment plus transport for 2 companies and 130 dependents — they own no DropShip. Yesterday {NPC:employer-contact} handed you the job: disarm and remove the rival outfit within 10 days, before {EMPLOYER}'s regular army arrives to do it with artillery and no idea how a foundry works. Attached to the job is the whole-complex security contract, pre-signed, on the condition that you deliver the north half 'secured and operational.' Operational is the key word. The foundry furnaces cannot be shut off fast — once a batch of metal is melting, it takes 14 hours to safely pour out, and if a furnace is breached everyone on the floor dies. The Spur costs 25,000 C-bills a day in penalties when it stops, charged to whoever is at fault. The rival commander {NPC:opfor-commander} answers your calls on the first ring — either professionalism, or a man counting his ammunition. Their cohesion is five unpaid weeks old and slipping, and who actually controls their second company has more than one answer (that report is 2 days old and rough).

objectives.primary: Deliver the north half secured and operational within 10 days — before {EMPLOYER}'s regular army arrives and solves the problem with artillery.
objectives.secondary: Keep the Common Spur running and the furnaces intact: no stoppage penalties charged to you, and no industrial disaster.
objectives.bonus: Resolve the rival outfit without spilling mercenary blood — the hiring halls judge outfits harshly for killing their own kind on an employer's schedule.

complications.name: The Greenline Memorandum
complications.text: Seven months of sharing the site means both outfits know each other's patrol schedules, callsigns, response times, and blind spots. The memorandum's safety rules around the furnaces are the one thing both sides still follow without argument. There is no surprise left in this complex — only the question of who breaks the rules first, and what that costs around molten metal.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Neither side can achieve surprise through normal moves; any attack is telegraphed 2-4 hours ahead unless it breaks the memorandum's furnace-safety rules — and any plan that does breaks them triggers the industrial-disaster risk in complication 3.

complications.name: No Exit Money
complications.text: The rival outfit's demand is not greed; it is math. Five weeks of unpaid wages, 130 dependents, no DropShip, no employer, and an outlawed paymaster whose accounts are frozen. Their commander is holding 2 companies together with reputation and rationed coffee. The longer the standoff drags, the less of the outfit stays under his command.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Each week of standoff, roll on rival cohesion. Results range from desertions (their strength drops, but deserters with inside knowledge go freelance nearby) to hardliner takeover (their second company stops obeying their commander — see DP 'The Hardliner Hour').

complications.name: The Works Keep Working
complications.text: Both the renewal contract and the penalty clause assume the complex keeps producing no matter what. A fight near the Spur stops the trains; a fight in the fabrication halls risks breaching a furnace; and a breach makes the whole question of who guards the north half pointless.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Combat within 400 m of the Common Spur stops rail traffic: 25,000 C-bills a day in penalties, charged to whoever is at fault. Combat inside the foundry halls while a batch is melting: roll against a furnace breach — on a breach, mass casualties, the north half prize is destroyed, and the renewal contract fails for good.

decisionPoints.name: The Tasking
decisionPoints.context: Ten days. The pre-signed renewal contract waits in its folder. {NPC:opfor-commander}'s outfit did nothing wrong except keep its word to an employer who lost — which, both commanders know, could someday be said of you instead. The regular army is coming either way.

options.title: Carry out the disarmament — plan the attack and take the north half
advantages: Decisive: you satisfy the renewal contract by your own hand, on your own schedule
{EMPLOYER} and the corporate board see exactly the tool they paid for
Done fast and cleanly, it beats both the hardliners and the regular army to the punch
disadvantages: You are attacking an outfit that knows your response times to the second, on ground full of furnaces and penalty clauses
Mercenaries evicting unpaid mercenaries for a contract is a story the hiring halls tell with names attached
Their dependents live in the north half housing blocks, so there is no attack plan without them in it
options.consequence: The complex's 7-month peace ends by your choice. Win or lose, the Greenline Memorandum becomes a thing people later call naive.

costs.resource: a projected 50,000-75,000 C-bills in stoppage penalties even in a clean operation, plus ammunition and repairs from your treasury
costs.risk: A reputation for evicting fellow mercenaries follows you for a decade, and you risk a furnace breach if the fight drifts north

options.title: Broker their exit — buy the receivable, front the lift
advantages: Bloodless: the north half changes hands by inventory checklist instead of gun camera

Buying their 5 weeks of unpaid wages at 40 percent and covering their transport turns 1,080,000 C-bills of your money into an enforceable legal claim, plus a survival debt owed by 2 companies of professionals
You satisfy the renewal contract with the foundries never missing a pour
disadvantages: 1,080,000 C-bills out the door against a legal claim on an outlawed duke's frozen accounts — your lawyer rates recovery as 'eventual, partial, or never'
{EMPLOYER} did not order generosity and will not repay it; the board may read it as you funding a rival's survival
If their hardliners reject the deal their commander shakes on, you have paid for a standoff you still have to resolve
options.consequence: The rival outfit leaves with its name intact and its debt acknowledged. You hold the whole complex, a thinner treasury, and a claim that pays out whenever justice does.

costs.risk: Recovering the money is uncertain, and the employer reads your independent dealmaking however it wants to

options.title: Stall — let the regular army arrive and do it themselves
advantages: Your hands stay clean of mercenary blood and your treasury stays closed
Whatever the regulars break, they break under their own flag and their own blame
No breach of your contract — you simply prove, with documentation, that you could not do it safely in time
disadvantages: Regulars solve industrial standoffs with artillery: the furnaces, the Spur, and the north half's 'operational' status are all on their target list
The renewal contract dies with whatever the shelling hits — and your claim to the whole-complex contract dies with it
{NPC:employer-contact} will note, in writing, that you needed the army to collect your own renewal
options.consequence: The problem gets solved by people with no stake in the prize. You keep your hands clean and lose the thing the 7 months were for.

costs.resource: the renewal contract is at severe risk: the regulars' methods versus 'secured and operational'
costs.risk: Employer relations drop by 2, and your reputation for handling hard jobs takes the quiet kind of damage

decisionPoints.name: The Hardliner Hour
decisionPoints.context: A private channel, 0300. {NPC:opfor-commander}, voice flat: their second company plans to seize foundry hall 2 at shift change and hold the furnaces hostage — threatening to breach them — until somebody pays. The commander offers you a joint action against his own mutineers, in exchange for the exit payment, personally guaranteed in writing, tonight. The batch in furnace 2 starts melting in 4 hours, and once it does, it cannot be safely stopped for 14.

options.title: Joint action — go in with the rival commander's loyal company
advantages: The loyalists know hall 2's catwalks, valve rooms, and the mutineers' faces — the difference between a clean raid and a massacre
Two outfits putting down a mutiny together is a story that buries the eviction story
The commander's demand for a guarantee is the exit deal you may want anyway, now priced by emergency
disadvantages: Armed troops of the force you were told to disarm, operating inside your own objective, on trust and a handshake
If it is fake — a staged mutiny to extract the guarantee — you have signed under pressure and armed the show
Crossfire risk in a foundry at shift change, between two outfits that have never fought on the same side
options.consequence: The mutiny is broken by the two commands that wrote the Greenline Memorandum, which is no longer naive afterward — but the guarantee you signed at 0300 is now the deal, whatever the board thinks.

costs.resource: the exit payment, personally guaranteed in writing — binding on you whether or not the employer reimburses it
costs.risk: Trust risk: rival loyalists armed inside your perimeter during the action

options.title: Strike the mutineers alone, before shift change
advantages: No leak from coordinating: the mutineers' inside knowledge helps the rival's loyalists too, and this route skips both
You control every gun in the plan — no crossfire risk, no exposure to a staged mutiny
Acting alone against the threat keeps the spirit of the job: the north half secured by your hand
disadvantages: You fight in hall 2 within 4 hours of the batch melting, against people who know which valves matter
The rival's loyal company is also armed, also at shift change, and has not agreed to stand aside for a foreign attack on their own people
Moving fast means breaking the memorandum's safety rules — exactly the risk complication 1 prices
options.consequence: The furnace question is settled by whoever reaches the valve room first. The rival commander learns you heard his offer and chose to treat his whole outfit as one target.

costs.resource: furnace-breach risk is active for the whole action
costs.risk: Two-front fight if the rival loyalists read your strike as the eviction starting; the memorandum is dead either way

options.title: Pay the mutineers' stall demand — 50,000 for 72 hours
advantages: The batch pours out safely; nobody fights in a foundry tonight
72 bought hours is enough to close either the brokered exit or a coordinated disarmament with the rival commander
By far the cheapest immediate option
disadvantages: Paying armed leverage teaches it the usual lesson: there is a second demand inside every first one
The employer will not reimburse a bribe and may treat it as you funding hostile forces inside the objective
The rival commander's authority — your only worthwhile negotiating partner — is publicly undercut the moment the mutineers get paid
options.consequence: You buy time at a steep cost: the mutineers are now a paid faction that knows the trick works, and every clock in the complex is 72 hours closer to the regular army.

costs.resource: the rival commander's authority is weakened — future talks run through a weaker partner
costs.risk: A second demand is likely, the employer will not reimburse it, and the precedent is priced into every later standoff

entries.event: The mutineer force (6-8 'Mechs and 20 on foot) moves on foundry hall 2 at shift change.
They seize the furnace control room and broadcast their terms on the complex-wide channel.
Furnace 2's batch starts melting — from here, pouring it out takes 14 hours, and interrupting it risks a breach.
The rival outfit's loyal company stands ready in the north yards, though even their commander is unsure which lances will obey.
The corporate board demands hourly updates, and {NPC:employer-contact} gently reminds you of the word 'operational.'
The pour finishes and the furnace hostage-hold ends — and everyone armed in the complex has known this hour all day.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Furnace 2's batch starts melting at T+0:30. From then until the pour finishes at T+14:30, any fight inside hall 2 risks a breach that kills everyone on the floor and destroys the renewal contract with them. Resolve the hall before the batch starts melting, or spend 14 hours negotiating with a hand on the valves.

opforSketch.composition: Rival outfit: 2 companies totaling 20-24 'Mechs (mixed weights, professionally maintained until the pay stopped), 4 support vehicles, organic infantry. Quality regular-to-veteran. The second company — the hardliner faction — holds 6-8 of those 'Mechs and the outfit's worst arrears grievances. Both companies trained joint exercises against the unit for 7 months: they know its doctrine the way it knows theirs.
opforSketch.behavior: The commander's loyalists fight only if attacked, and fight to negotiate — they want exit, not victory. The hardliners fight for leverage: seizures, threats, and short violent demonstrations near the things both employers value. Nobody in the north half wants to die for a proscribed duke; everybody in it has dependents in the housing blocks, which is both restraint and desperation.

forks.name: OPERATION WHOLE CLOTH
forks.trigger: North half delivered secured and operational; consolidated contract executed
forks.consequence: The unit guards the whole complex now — twice the perimeter, twice the rate, and the losing claimant's stay-behind networks shifting their full attention to the one outfit holding the prize they could not keep.

forks.name: OPERATION OLD COLLEAGUES
forks.trigger: Rival outfit shattered by force — survivors scatter armed and unpaid
forks.consequence: Eight to twelve 'Mechs of ex-professionals who know every patrol schedule, dead zone, and supply run in the district go raider inside a month. The board contracts the unit to hunt the people it broke, and the hiring halls watch how it conducts itself with very particular attention.

forks.name: OPERATION REFERENCE CHECK
forks.trigger: Eviction executed with mercenary blood and the story travels (it always travels)
forks.consequence: The renewal pays, and then the market answers: three straight tender rejections with no reasons given. The only paper on offer is a flat-rate garrison on a periphery transfer world nobody wants — where the unit can be useful, profitable, and quietly forgotten until the ledger entry fades.

storyElementSeed: Two duty officers from different payrolls meet at the rail interlocking at shift change, swap thermos cups the way they have for 7 months, and neither mentions the new ammunition crates both signed for this week.

resourceGates.appliesTo: Broker their exit — buy the receivable, front the lift
resourceGates.lackingText: Treasury short of the brokered package: the option reprices as a financing request to the conglomerate board — which means revealing the plan to an employer who ordered an eviction, and taking the board's answer as part of the deal.

resourceGates.appliesTo: Broker their exit — buy the receivable, front the lift
resourceGates.lackingText: No unit hulls to lend: the rival's lift requires commercial charter — 600,000 C-bills, 12-day lead time. The brief prints the charter lead time beside the regulars' arrival estimate, and the two numbers do not get along.

skeleton: two hired companies guarding adjacent halves of one working prize must keep a professional rivalry inside contract bounds until one employer's proscription converts the rival into the assigned target — and the order to disarm yesterday's colleagues arrives stapled to the renewal both outfits wanted
inspiration: rival condottieri companies in a single city-state's pay — the Braccio-Sforza feud, and the disarmament commissions that ended such standoffs

title: OPERATION WITNESS FEE
situation: Your campaign behind {TARGET_FACTION}'s lines on {WORLD} runs on Annex D, and Annex D runs on witnesses. {EMPLOYER}'s regional command pays only for confirmed results: 40,000 C-bills per supply convoy destroyed, 70,000 per fuel or ammunition dump, 150,000 per BattleMech, 300,000 per fighter. But you only get the full rate when the employer's field assessor certifies the result in person. Gun-camera footage alone pays half — the contract calls this the 'technical means discount.' The catch is the deniability clause right next to the pay schedule: you fight under resistance colors, with no link to the employer, and the employer will deny you if you're captured. Nobody says the obvious out loud: the assessor, {NPC:employer-contact}, is plainly a House officer — House bearing, House boots, House radio gear — so every strike they show up to certify is itself a breach of the deniability everyone is paid to protect. Your safe haven is the Lantern Fens: 1,900 square km of peat bog where a crossing 'Mech leaves a trail visible from the air for 6 hours, so every strike has to fit inside the 4-to-9-hour gaps between air patrols (from 31 days of tracking their patterns). Bringing the assessor's party along adds 90 minutes to every leg. Twenty-three strikes in, your ledger reads: 9 claims paid in full, 8 paid at half, and 6 denied outright for 'insufficient persistence of effect' — meaning two trucks limped away from a dead convoy, or a dump was rebuilt from spare stock inside the 72-hour window the contract requires damage to last. {NPC:intel-source}, a clerk in the command's payment office, reports that the denial rate tracks the employer's quarterly budget cycle to within a week (that report is 12 days old and rough). This season's prize is now on the table: a battalion ammunition transfer point at the fen's eastern edge, worth 240,000 C-bills at the full rate or 120,000 at the discount — and the deepest risk you have taken yet. The occupation garrison, a sector battalion with a fighter pair on call, has started flying its patrols with shorter gaps; that report is 4 days old and solid. Your campaign only stays solvent at full rates. Full rates require the witness. The witness is the risk, and that risk falls on the fens — the only home your campaign has.

objectives.primary: Destroy the eastern-edge ammunition transfer point so the damage lasts beyond the contract's 72-hour verification window.
objectives.secondary: Protect the safe haven: leave no trail leading home and nothing traceable to the fen base.
objectives.bonus: End the quarter with your claims paid in full — by a witness, by neutral verification, or by evidence the payment office cannot argue with.

complications.name: The Technical Means Discount
complications.text: Proof determines payment. Gun-camera footage alone earns only half the contract value — the employer wants a witness, not just a recording. Bringing the field assessor along to verify the strike earns full payment, but at a price: the assessor slows the team down, makes the force easier to detect, and puts a House officer inside an operation that is supposed to be deniable. Annex D never explains how a campaign can be both deniable and audited at once, because it cannot.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Before each strike, choose whether to bring the assessor. Without the assessor: move at full speed and receive 50 percent payment. With the assessor: add 90 minutes to each movement leg and raise compromise risk by one level during infiltration and extraction, but receive full payment if the strike succeeds while the assessor is present to witness it.

complications.name: Persistence of Effect
complications.text: Destroying a target is only half the job. The damage must last. A successful strike is one that keeps the enemy from recovering for at least 72 hours: supply convoys must stay disabled, supply dumps must remain unusable, and wrecked equipment should still be sitting where it fell. If the enemy repairs or replaces what was destroyed before then, the strike does not pay. To confirm an effect held, reconnaissance teams may need to return to the strike site about three days later — a dangerous follow-up, because the enemy expects someone to come back and will be watching the ground precisely because it was hit.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A strike that only partially damages its target pays nothing. Any claim that the enemy might rebuild or reconstitute requires a verification revisit 72 hours later — a separate exposure roll on ground the enemy is now guarding because it was struck once already.

complications.name: Wakes in the Peat
complications.text: The peat fens hide movement well, but heavy machines leave traces a skilled observer can find. Every 'Mech that crosses the wetland churns a visible path that can be spotted from the air for up to six hours afterward. Because of this, infiltration and extraction must be timed to fit inside the gaps between enemy air patrols — and those gaps are getting shorter every month. If the force is still moving after a gap closes, the fresh trail leads the patrol straight back toward the campaign's hidden base.
complications.mechanicalEffect: All movement in the fens must be completed inside a single patrol gap (rolled at 4-9 hours). An extraction trail stays readable from the air for 6 hours after the last movement leg. If the gap closes before that trail fades, the patrol overflies it and the base-compromise track advances one step.

decisionPoints.name: Pricing the Witness
decisionPoints.context: You have planned the transfer-point strike two ways. The fast plan fits the average patrol gap with 40 minutes to spare and pays 120,000. The witnessed plan only fits if the gap runs long, and pays 240,000 — the difference between a solvent quarter and a borrowed one. The assessor waits at the rally point for your answer, House boots already oiled.

options.title: Take the assessor — full rate, thin margins
advantages: 240,000 C-bills confirmed on the spot: no discount, no dispute, no budget-cycle games
An assessor who walked the strike in person defends the claim in the payment office — this one and the next
Full payment on the season's prize keeps the campaign solvent for a quarter
disadvantages: Your party moves 90 minutes slower through gaps that have been shrinking for a month
A House officer captured or killed at a resistance-flagged strike site blows the deniability clause and everything built on it
If the gap closes early, your trail leads the patrol home — the safe haven pays for the payday
options.consequence: The strike is verified as it happens, by the one witness the employer cannot discount — carried through the fens at the campaign's own risk.

costs.resource: you use up nearly all your patrol-gap margin, leaving no slack in the escape timing
costs.risk: Losing the assessor collapses your deniability (COMPROMISED fork); an early gap closure advances the base-compromise track

options.title: Go without — fast, safe, half pay
advantages: The fast plan fits the average gap with real margin, so your safe haven is at its lowest risk in weeks
No House signature anywhere near the strike, so the deniability clause stays airtight
120,000 C-bills is still your biggest single claim this quarter
disadvantages: The half rate is not the worst case: denials hit hardest at the budget quarter's final month, and this is that month
A campaign that stops buying witnesses teaches the employer that 50 percent is the price of everything
At half rates, the math says the campaign folds in 60 to 75 days no matter how well you shoot
options.consequence: The strike succeeds quietly and goes into the ledger as an argument instead of a fact. The payment office sharpens its pencil.

costs.resource: you lose 120,000 C-bills versus the witnessed rate, before any denial risk
costs.risk: The footage-only claim faces the quarter-end denial pattern; projected payout 60,000-120,000

options.title: Demand pre-certification — sensors placed, assessor at the rally point, terms in writing
advantages: This new arrangement splits the difference: your placed sensor records count as a witness, and the assessor signs off before the strike
Full rate without carrying House boots to the objective
It sets up a verification method the whole campaign can reuse — the precedent is worth more than the strike
disadvantages: The assessor has to sign for results they will not see, and assessors who do that want cover — the price comes right away
The price: the assessor wants you to plant a House sensor suite at the transfer site during the strike, sneaking the employer's own spy job into your operation, with the attribution risk that carries
If the payment office rejects the new arrangement afterward anyway, you carried the extra gear for a discount
options.consequence: The verification problem gets a technical fix, and the mission grows a second, unwritten objective. You are now doing spy work you never priced, for a signature you had already earned.

costs.resource: you add 1 House sensor suite to plant at the objective (extra to carry, extra time, attribution risk)
costs.risk: The payment office may reject the new arrangement, and the smuggled spy job is deniable by everyone except you, the one carrying it

decisionPoints.name: The Sixth Denial
decisionPoints.context: The denial hits your best single claim: a {TARGET_FACTION} BattleMech, killed clean in the western fen — then swallowed by the bog before the 72-hour window closed. 'No lasting wreck available to assess.' 150,000 C-bills, refused in one form sentence. The machine is eleven meters down in airless mud: perfectly preserved, impossible to reach, and completely real.

options.title: Raise the wreck — prove the claim with a derrick and five days
advantages: A recovered wreck can't be argued with: full claim paid, plus the salvage itself — bog-preserved Star League-era parts sell no matter what the ledger says
The recovery also sends the payment office a message about how far you will go to collect
Digging deep in the fen is invisible to road patrols — only the air can see it
disadvantages: Five days of stationary derrick work under a tarp, in country where trails stay visible for 6 hours and patrol gaps are shrinking
A fixed site you return to daily is exactly the pattern the occupation's analysts are paid to spot
If the air finds the derrick, you have spent your safe haven's safety margin to prove a 150,000 C-bill point
options.consequence: The claim becomes physical, and so does the risk: your books improve at the exact rate your base-compromise track worsens.

costs.resource: your derrick party sits at one site for 5 days, and the base-compromise track rises 1 per day it is overflown
costs.risk: A fixed target in shrinking gaps; discovery turns a pay dispute into a hunt for your base

options.title: Invoke the neutral-verification rider — a ComStar adjudicator
advantages: The clause exists for exactly this: a neutral ComStar official reviews the gun-camera, the sonar trace, and the burial site, and their ruling binds both sides
No derrick, no days sitting still — how the official proves it is their problem, not yours
A binding ruling breaks the denial pattern for every claim after this one; the budget cycle loses its favorite tool
disadvantages: A ComStar official travels openly, asks questions in writing, and files reports you will never see — so details of a deniable campaign now sit in a third party's archive
A 30,000 C-bill fee against a 150,000 claim, win or lose
{EMPLOYER} reads this as escalation, and the assessor's office turns openly hostile for the rest of the campaign
options.consequence: The claim is probably paid and the campaign is certainly watched. Once you invite ComStar's interest, it does not announce when it leaves.

costs.risk: A different kind of exposure: ComStar's archive now holds your campaign, and employer relations harden

options.title: Eat the denial — aim the campaign at targets no one can deny
advantages: Dropped bridges, burned pumping stations, cut rail lines on the trunk line: results no 72-hour window can argue with and no assessor has to walk to
The denial game ends because the kind of evidence changes — infrastructure does not limp away or get rebuilt overnight
No extra risk spent on the dead claim; the bog keeps the 'Mech and the argument
disadvantages: Undeniable means visible: public damage triggers the occupation's reprisal policy, and reprisals fall on the fen-edge settlements whose silence hides you
Infrastructure strikes drift the campaign from harassment toward destruction — a different war than the one you signed up for, with a heavier weight on your conscience
The 150,000 stays unpaid, and the payment office learns that denial works
options.consequence: Your books balance going forward on a darker target list. You solve the verification problem by becoming the kind of campaign whose results everyone can see — including the people you hide among.

costs.resource: you write off the 150,000 C-bill claim
costs.risk: Reprisals shift onto fen-edge civilians, and your safe haven's human cover erodes as the damage becomes public

entries.event: Alarm at the transfer point; the site defense (an infantry platoon and 2 turrets) stands to.
The sector battalion's duty company is alerted; its wheeled element starts up the fen road, 26 km out.
A fighter pair takes off from the sector field and makes its first pass over the eastern edge.
The reaction company reaches the transfer point; pursuers probe the fen margin but will not enter the bog at night.
Your escape trail fades — the last fen leg stops being visible from the air.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Your escape trail stays visible from the air for 6 hours after your last movement leg in the fens. If the patrol gap closes before you reach cover under the eastern tree canopy, the patrol follows the fresh trail back toward your hidden base — the one thing this campaign cannot replace.

opforSketch.composition: {TARGET_FACTION} occupation sector: 1 garrison battalion (1 'Mech company of 10-12 machines, regular; motorized infantry; engineer platoon rebuilding what the campaign breaks), 1 aerospace pair on call with a second pair 3 days' transfer away. Static site defenses at logistics nodes: infantry platoons and automated turrets.
opforSketch.behavior: Occupation economy-of-force: pattern patrols, signature analysis, patience. They do not chase into the peat; they map wakes, tighten gaps, and wait for the campaign to repeat itself. Reprisal doctrine activates only against publicly visible effects — the garrison's political officers prefer an invisible war too.

forks.name: OPERATION PAID INVOICE
forks.trigger: Transload point destroyed with persistence; quarter's ledger settled at or near full rates
forks.consequence: The campaign's arithmetic finally forces {TARGET_FACTION} to garrison its logistics in depth — and {EMPLOYER}, reading the same arithmetic, offers the proven unit the sector airfield itself: the aerospace pair on the ground, at a rate that for once nobody discounts.

forks.name: OPERATION PEAT SMOKE
forks.trigger: Base-compromise track filled — the occupation fixes the fen base's location
forks.consequence: The fen base's location is compromised, and it is now only a matter of time before the occupation acts on it. The unit must mount a loud, sustained deception campaign at the fen's far margin — strikes whose only purpose is to be seen — while the real base relocates piece by piece under the cover that noise buys.

forks.name: OPERATION ORPHAN FLAG
forks.trigger: The assessor captured at or near a strike site
forks.consequence: The employer disavows the unit by reflex and, in the same encrypted breath, offers a recovery bonus for the assessor — whose interrogation will unravel the denial of a contract that officially never existed. The unit is hired to rescue the proof that it was never hired.

storyElementSeed: An assessor in borrowed local clothes initials three lines of a claim sheet by red lamplight, turns the fourth line face down, and says nothing while the rain works on the tent.

resourceGates.appliesTo: Raise the wreck — prove the claim with a derrick and five days
resourceGates.lackingText: You have no heavy recovery gear in the fen caches, so the derrick is rigged from logging equipment: 5 days become 8, and every added day is another trail the air can spot. The brief prints the new day count next to the patrol-gap trend line.

resourceGates.appliesTo: Invoke the neutral-verification rider — a ComStar adjudicator
resourceGates.lackingText: You cannot afford the fee, so ComStar bills {EMPLOYER} directly — who then takes it out of your next paid claim at double the amount, under an Annex D cost-recovery line nobody read twice.

skeleton: a hidden force is paid only for effects its employer's own assessor certifies, but the assessor's presence is itself the deniability breach the contract forbids and every denial saves the employer money — the campaign's books and its cover degrade on the same schedule
inspiration: the American Volunteer Group's confirmed-kill bonus system and its verification disputes — the Flying Tigers' pay ledger
